title: Surveying
description: Chain and compass surveying, levelling, contouring, plane table and theodolite work, tacheometry, curves, traverse computations, areas and volumes, and advanced topics including remote sensing, GIS, GPS, and astronomical surveying.

questions.text: Which one of the following closely represents the shape of the earth?
questions.expl: The earth is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator due to rotation, making an oblate spheroid the closest approximation to its true shape.

questions.text: Hydrographic survey deals with the mapping of
questions.expl: Hydrographic surveying is the branch of surveying concerned with mapping large water bodies such as seas, lakes, and rivers, including their shorelines and depths.

questions.text: The survey in which the curvature of the earth is taken into account is called
questions.expl: Geodetic surveys cover very large areas and explicitly account for the earth's curvature, unlike plane surveys which assume a flat reference surface.

questions.text: The survey in which the curvature of the earth is ignored is called
questions.expl: A plane survey treats the surveyed area as a flat plane and neglects the earth's curvature, which is valid for smaller areas.

questions.text: The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is
questions.expl: By convention, curvature effects become significant and must be considered once the surveyed area exceeds about 260 sq. km.

questions.text: The survey done to fix property lines and to calculate land area for transfer of land property from one owner to another is known as
questions.expl: Cadastral surveys are conducted specifically to establish property boundaries and land parcels for ownership and legal transfer purposes.

questions.text: The effect of curvature of the earth is neglected in case the area to be surveyed is less than
questions.expl: This is the same 260 sq. km threshold below which plane surveying (ignoring curvature) is considered accurate enough.

questions.text: Geodetic surveying is different from plane surveying because of
options: The large difference of elevations between various points
Coverage of a very large area
questions.expl: The defining distinction between geodetic and plane surveying is that geodetic surveying accounts for the earth's curvature while plane surveying does not.

questions.text: The principle of 'working from whole to part' is used in surveying because
options: Survey work can be completed quickly
questions.expl: Establishing a framework of accurate control points first, then filling in details, localizes and prevents the accumulation and magnification of errors across the survey.

questions.text: A survey in which the horizontal and vertical locations of points are fixed by linear and angular measurement is known as
questions.expl: Topographical surveys determine both the horizontal positions and elevations (vertical locations) of ground features using linear and angular measurements.

questions.text: The error which occurs while conducting the survey from whole to part and part to whole is
options: In whole to part, it is localized, and in part to whole, it is expanded
In whole to part, it is expanded, and in part to whole, it is localized
In both the methods, the error is localized
questions.expl: Working from whole to part confines errors to small, localized parts of the survey, whereas working from part to whole causes errors to accumulate and expand outward.

questions.text: Which one of the following surveys is required for the observation of stars?
questions.expl: Astronomical surveying uses observations of celestial bodies (stars, sun) to determine position, azimuth, and time.

questions.text: Which one of the following surveys is employed for collecting sufficient data in connection with sewage disposal and water supply works?
questions.expl: City surveys are carried out for urban infrastructure planning purposes, including sewage disposal and water supply system design.

questions.text: Preliminary survey of an area is called
questions.expl: A reconnaissance survey is a rapid preliminary examination of an area carried out before detailed survey work begins, to plan the survey layout.

questions.text: Which one of the following conditions requires geodetic surveying?
questions.expl: Surveying an entire country covers an area large enough that the earth's curvature must be accounted for, requiring geodetic methods.

questions.text: A plan is a graphical representation of features on a large scale as projected on a
questions.expl: A plan represents ground features by orthogonal projection onto a horizontal plane, distinguishing it from elevations or sections.

questions.text: Systematic errors are those errors
options: Whose effects are cumulative and can be eliminated by adopting suitable methods
questions.expl: Systematic errors follow a definite mathematical or physical law, so their cumulative effect can be predicted, corrected, or eliminated through proper technique.

questions.text: Theory of probability is applied to
questions.expl: Accidental (random) errors follow no fixed law and are governed by chance, so the theory of probability is used to analyze and adjust them.

questions.text: The difference between the true value of a quantity and its observed value is
questions.expl: By definition, the true error is the difference between an observation and the (usually unknown) true value of the quantity.

questions.text: Which of the following scales is the largest one?
questions.expl: Converting all to representative fraction: 1 cm = 50 m gives RF = 1/5000, which is a larger scale (bigger RF value) than 1/42000, 1/300000, or 1 cm = 50 km (RF = 1/5,000,000).

questions.text: The order of precision required in survey work mainly depends upon the
questions.expl: For high-precision geodetic and control surveys, an accuracy order of about 1 in 100,000 is typically specified as the required standard.

questions.text: The smallest length that can be drawn on a map is
questions.expl: The generally accepted smallest distinguishable length that can be plotted and read on a map by the naked eye is taken as 0.5 mm (0.25 mm is the plotting limit, 0.5 mm the reading limit conventionally used).

questions.text:
Surveying is the art of determining the relative positions of points on, above or beneath the surface of the earth, with respect to each other, by the measurement of
(i) Distances
(ii) Directions
(iii) Elevations
questions.expl: Surveying fundamentally relies on measuring distances, directions, and elevations together to fix the relative positions of points.

questions.text:
The objective of a survey is to
(i) Prepare a plan or map
(ii) Determine the relative position of points
(iii) Determine position of points in a horizontal plane
(iv) Determine position of points in a vertical plane
questions.expl: Surveying aims to prepare a plan and fix the relative positions of points in both horizontal and vertical planes, so all four objectives apply.

questions.text: The difference between the most probable value of a quantity and its observed value is
questions.expl: The residual error is defined as the difference between the most probable value (the best estimate from adjustment) and an individual observed value.

questions.text: Ranging is defined as
options: Measuring the distance from starting point
Establishing intermediate points on a chain line
A point on a chain line
questions.expl: Ranging is the process of fixing intermediate points along a chain line so that the surveyed line remains straight between its end stations.

questions.text: The process of fixing intermediate points is called
questions.expl: Fixing intermediate points on a straight survey line, so the chain can follow a straight path, is called ranging.

questions.text: The error due to bad ranging is
questions.expl: Poor ranging causes the chain line to bow, always making the measured distance longer than the true straight-line distance, so the error is cumulative and negative (the true length is overstated).

questions.text: 'Ranging' is the process of
options: Fixing ranging rods on the extremities of the area
Aligning the chain in a straight line
Taking offsets from a chain line
Chaining over a range of mountains
questions.expl: Ranging keeps the chain aligned in a straight line between the end stations of a survey line.

questions.text: An obstacle which obstructs chaining but not ranging may be a
questions.expl: A lake blocks physical chaining across it but the ends can still be seen and ranging rods can still be sighted across the water, so ranging is unobstructed.

questions.text: The length of a ranging rod should be
questions.expl: Standard ranging rods are made in lengths typically between 2 m and 3 m for ordinary use, extending up to about 4.5 m for taller/longer variants, so the practical range is 2.5-4.5 m as commonly specified.

questions.text: The longest chain line passing through the centre of the area is known as
questions.expl: The base line is the main, longest chain line run through the survey area, from which the framework of triangles is built.

questions.text: A line joining some fixed points on the survey lines is called
questions.expl: A tie line joins two fixed points on the main survey lines and is used to take offsets for detail or as a check on the main framework.

questions.text: 'Offsets' are
options: Ties or check lines which are perpendicular to the chain line
Sets of minor measurements in chain surveying
Chain lines which go out of alignment
questions.expl: Offsets are the lateral (sideways) measurements taken from the chain line to locate nearby details.

questions.text: The maximum length of an offset depends on
questions.expl: The permissible offset length is governed by the scale of the map being plotted, since it limits the plotting accuracy of offset details.

questions.text: Offsets are
options: Short measurements from a chain line
Ties or check lines which are perpendicular to the chain line
Sets of minor instruments in chain surveying
Chain lines which go out of alignment
questions.expl: Offsets are short lateral measurements taken from the chain line to fix the position of objects or boundary points.

questions.text: As per Indian Standard, the length of one link in a 30 m chain should be (in cm)
questions.expl: A 30 m (metric) chain consists of 150 links, and 30 m / 150 = 0.20 m, so each link is 20 cm long.

questions.text: Invar tape is used for accurate measurement of distances because
options: Its coefficient of thermal expansion is low
Its coefficient of thermal expansion is zero
It does not break on twisting or bending
It is light in weight and good in strength
questions.expl: Invar (an alloy of nickel and steel) has a very low coefficient of thermal expansion, so its length changes negligibly with temperature, making it suitable for precise baseline measurement.

questions.text: For determination of the area of land having straight line boundaries, the land figure is converted into
questions.expl: Straight-boundary land areas are conventionally divided into a series of triangles, whose individual areas are then computed and summed.

questions.text: The maximum tolerance in a 20 m chain is
questions.expl: As per Indian Standard specifications, a 20 m chain is permitted a maximum tolerance of about ±5 mm.

questions.text: The number of links in a 30 m metric chain is
questions.expl: A 30 m metric chain is made of 150 links, each link therefore being 20 cm long.

questions.text: Adjustment of a too-long chain is done by
options: Replacing old rings with new ones
questions.expl: A chain that has stretched too long can be corrected by any combination of reshaping worn rings, closing opened joints, or replacing rings, so all listed methods apply.

questions.text: The distance between two posts measured with a 20 m chain was found to be 250 m. If the chain is 10 cm too long, then the true distance between the posts is
questions.expl: True length = measured length × (actual chain length / nominal length) = 250 × (20.10/20) = 251.25 m, since a too-long chain understates the number of chain-lengths needed but each recorded length is actually longer.

questions.text: The main object of running a tie line is
options: To take details of nearby objects
To take offsets for detailed surveying
questions.expl: Tie lines are primarily run to locate interior details near the main survey lines by taking offsets from them.

questions.text: The true length of a line is known to be 200 m. When measured with a 20 m tape, the length is 200.80 m. The correct length of the 20 m tape is
questions.expl: Number of tape lengths used = 200.80/20 = 10.04, and true length per tape length = 200/10.04 ≈ 20.08 m, so the tape's actual length is 20.08 m.

questions.text: A 30 m metric chain is found to be 0.1 m too short throughout the measurement. If the distance measured is recorded as 300 m, then the actual distance will be
questions.expl: True distance = measured distance × (actual chain length/nominal length) = 300 × (29.9/30) = 299.0 m, since a too-short chain makes the recorded distance overstate the true distance.

questions.text: The permissible error in chaining for measurement on rough or hilly ground is
questions.expl: For rough or hilly terrain, the accepted permissible error in chaining is relaxed to about 1 in 250, compared to tighter tolerances on smooth ground.

questions.text: What is the slope correction for a length of 30 m along a gradient of 1 in 20?
questions.expl: Slope correction ≈ h²/2L, where h = 30/20 = 1.5 m, giving correction = 1.5²/(2×30) = 0.0375 m = 3.75 cm.

questions.text: Compensating errors in chaining are
options: Proportional to the length of the line
Proportional to the square root of the length of the line
Inversely proportional to the square root of the length of the line
Inversely proportional to the length of the line
questions.expl: Random (compensating) errors accumulate according to the laws of probability, so their combined effect grows with the square root of the number of measurements, i.e., the square root of the line length.

questions.text: The accuracy of measurement in chain surveying does not depend upon
questions.expl: All three listed factors (offset length, importance of features, plotting scale) do influence accuracy in chain surveying, so 'none of these' is correct as the exception.

questions.text: The error in measured length due to sag of a chain or tape is known as
questions.expl: Sag causes the chain/tape to hang in a catenary curve, shortening the horizontal distance actually spanned, so the correction is subtracted, meaning the raw error is termed a positive (too-long) error.

questions.text: Sag correction is applicable while using
options: A dumpy level on sloping ground
A plane table by the two-point problem
questions.expl: Sag correction applies to tape measurements taken with the tape suspended in catenary between supports, not touching the ground throughout.

questions.text: The correction for sag is
questions.expl: Sag always causes the tape to record a length longer than the true horizontal distance, so the sag correction is always subtracted (negative).

questions.text: The number of independent conditions required to be satisfied for the adjustment of a braced quadrilateral in triangulation survey is
questions.expl: A braced quadrilateral requires satisfying four independent geometric conditions (typically one figure condition and three or four side/angle conditions) as per standard triangulation adjustment practice.

questions.text: A 20 m chain was found to be 10 cm too long after chaining a distance of 2000 m. It was found to be 18 cm too long at the end of the day's work, after chaining a total distance of 4000 m. What is the true distance if the chain was correct before the commencement of the day's work?
questions.expl: Treating the elongation as uniform within each segment and using the average excess: first 2000 m (excess 0 to 10 cm, average 5 cm) gives true = 2000×(20.05/20) = 2005 m; next 2000 m (excess 10 to 18 cm, average 14 cm) gives true = 2000×(20.14/20) = 2014 m; total true distance = 2005 + 2014 = 4019 m.

questions.text: A 30 m chain, after measuring a distance of 6000 m, was found to be 10 cm more than the designated length. If the chain was standardized before the commencement of the survey, the true length is
questions.expl: True length = measured length × (final chain length/nominal length) = 6000 × (30.10/30) = 6020 m, applying the excess found at the end of the measurement to the whole recorded distance.

questions.text: Correct length of a 50 m tape, weighing 1.2 kg, when a pull of 12 kg is applied at the ends and it is freely suspended, is
questions.expl: This applies the sag correction formula (Cs = W²L/24P²) for a freely suspended tape under an applied pull, which reduces the effective length below the nominal 50 m, giving approximately 49.98 m.

questions.text: A cross-staff is used for
questions.expl: A cross-staff is a simple optical instrument used solely to set out perpendicular (right-angle) offsets from a chain line.

questions.text: Chainage in chain survey means
options: The perpendicular distance of the object from the chain line
The distance of the object along the chain line from the zero end of the chain
Any distance measured by chain in field
questions.expl: Chainage refers to the distance measured along the chain line from the starting (zero) point to a given point or object's foot of perpendicular.

questions.text: Main stations in chain survey are the points
options: Lying in the area enclosed by survey lines
On main survey lines to cover the local details
On main survey lines to check the accuracy of the survey work
questions.expl: Main stations are the control points at the ends of the main survey lines that form the skeleton framework of the survey.

questions.text: Oblique offsets are used to
options: Check the accuracy of the plotted work in chain survey
questions.expl: Oblique offsets (taken at angles other than 90°, tied by two measurements) are primarily used to verify or check the accuracy of the plotted work.

questions.text: While measuring horizontal distance with a chain on hills, it is better to measure the distance by
questions.expl: Stepping is easier and more accurate when working downhill, so stepping down the slope is the preferred method for chaining on hilly ground.

questions.text: Prolongation of a chain line across an obstruction in chain survey is done by
questions.expl: Various geometric methods (angular observation, perpendicular offsets, or triangle construction) can all be used to prolong a chain line past an obstacle, so all apply.

questions.text: While measuring a line between two stations A and B intervened by a raised ground,
options: Vision and chaining both get obstructed
questions.expl: A raised ground (like a hillock) blocks the line of sight between the stations while the ground surface is still physically chainable, so only vision is obstructed.

questions.text: The correction to be applied to each 30 m chain length along a slope of angle α is
questions.expl: The slope correction subtracted from the measured slope length L to get the horizontal length is L(1 − cos α), which for L = 30 m gives 30(1 − cos α).

questions.text: Perpendicularity of an offset may be judged by eye if the length of the offset is less than
questions.expl: For very short offsets, up to about 5 m, a right angle can be judged reliably by eye without an optical instrument.

questions.text: Invar tape is made of an alloy of
questions.expl: Invar is an alloy of nickel and steel, specifically formulated to have a very low coefficient of thermal expansion.

questions.text: The length of a chain is measured from the
options: Centre of one handle to the centre of other handle
Outside of one handle to the outside of other handle
Outside of one handle to the inside of other handle
Inside of one handle to the inside of other handle
questions.expl: By convention, the designated length of a surveyor's chain is measured from the outside of one handle to the outside of the other handle.

questions.text: The angle of intersection of the two plain mirrors of an optical square is
questions.expl: In an optical square, the two mirrors are set at 45° to each other, which by the law of reflection deflects the line of sight by 90°.

questions.text: Which of the following angles can be set out with the help of a French cross-staff?
questions.expl: A French (adjustable) cross-staff has slits arranged to set out both 90° and 45° angles, unlike the simple cross-staff which only gives 90°.

questions.text: If the length of a chain is found to be short on testing, it can be adjusted by
options: Removing one or more small circular rings and placing bigger rings
Closing the joints of the rings, if opened
questions.expl: A chain found too short can be lengthened by straightening bent links, inserting larger rings, or closing gaps at joints, so all of these methods are valid.

questions.text: The position of a point can be fixed accurately by
questions.expl: An optical square, using mirror reflection principles, sets out perpendiculars far more accurately than a simple cross-staff, making it the more accurate instrument for fixing a point's position.

questions.text: Which of the following is an obstacle to chaining but not to ranging?
questions.expl: A river blocks direct chaining across it, but since both banks remain visible, ranging rods can still be sighted across, so ranging is unaffected.

questions.text: A building is an obstacle to
questions.expl: A building blocks both the physical passage of the chain and the line of sight needed for ranging, so it obstructs both operations.

questions.text: Which of the following is not used in measuring perpendicular offsets?
questions.expl: A line ranger is used to align points on a straight line, not to set out or measure perpendicular offsets, so it is the odd one out.

questions.text: The main difference between an optical square and a prism square is
options: The difference in the principle of working
That an optical square is more accurate than a prism square
That no adjustment is required in a prism square since the angle between the reflecting surfaces cannot be changed
questions.expl: A prism square is a single solid glass prism with a fixed reflecting angle that cannot go out of adjustment, unlike an optical square with separate mirrors that may need adjustment.

questions.text: The allowable length of an offset depends upon the
options: Method of setting out the perpendicular and nature of ground
questions.expl: The permissible offset length is governed jointly by the required accuracy, the method used to set it out, ground conditions, and the plotting scale, so all listed factors apply.

questions.text: Pick up the correct statement.
options: A revenue chain is 66 ft long
A tally is used to facilitate observation in an optical square
A brass ring is provided at every metre length in a metric chain
questions.expl: In a metric chain, a small brass ring/tag is fixed at every metre length to help identify readings quickly, making this the correct statement (the revenue chain is actually 33 ft, and Gunter devised the Gunter's chain, not invar tape).

questions.text: The most accurate instrument of the following for making linear measurements is
questions.expl: Invar tape, due to its very low thermal expansion coefficient, gives the highest accuracy among chains, steel bands, and steel tapes for linear measurement.

questions.text: Reciprocal ranging is adopted when the following is encountered
questions.expl: Reciprocal ranging is used when the end stations of a line are not intervisible due to intervening high ground such as a hillock, requiring surveyors to guide each other alternately.

questions.text: The measured length of a line was 1000 m, with a 30 m tape which was exactly 30 m at 27°C. If α = 1.20 × 10⁻⁵/°C and the field temperature is 37°C, the correct length in metres is
questions.expl: Temperature correction = L·α·ΔT = 1000 × 1.20×10⁻⁵ × 10 = 0.12 m; since the field temperature is higher, the tape expands and the true length is longer, giving 1000.12 m.

questions.text: An example of an obstacle to both chaining and ranging is
questions.expl: A river obstructs both physical chaining across it and, if wide enough, line-of-sight ranging, making it a classic obstacle to both operations in this context.

questions.text: Pick up the incorrect pair.
questions.expl: Plasterer's laths are used to mark the alignment/position of ranging points, not specifically as terminal-point markers in the sense implied, making this pairing the incorrect one per the answer key.

questions.text: A horizontal angle which a line makes with the true meridian through one of the extremities of the line, is called
questions.expl: When the reference meridian used is the true (geographic) meridian, the horizontal angle measured is specifically called the true bearing.

questions.text: The angle between the true meridian and magnetic meridian at the time of observation is known as
questions.expl: Magnetic declination is defined precisely as the horizontal angle between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place at a given time.

questions.text: Local attraction in compass surveying occurs due to
options: Loss of magnetism of the needle
Friction of the needle at the pivot
questions.expl: Local attraction is caused by nearby magnetic materials (iron objects, electric cables, etc.) that deflect the compass needle from the true magnetic meridian.

questions.text: Due to local attraction, -- is disturbed
questions.expl: Local attraction deflects the compass needle, which directly disturbs the observed bearing of the line being surveyed.

questions.text: The magnetic needle in a prismatic compass is placed
options: At the bottom of the graduated aluminium ring
Below the needle lifter, but above the bottom inside the compass
questions.expl: In a prismatic compass, the magnetic needle is mounted at the bottom of, and beneath, the graduated aluminium ring so it can freely align with the magnetic meridian.

questions.text: The variation in magnetic declination is
questions.expl: The magnetic declination at a place changes over the course of a day; this daily fluctuation is termed diurnal variation.

questions.text: The temporary adjustment of a prismatic compass is
questions.expl: Centering the instrument exactly over the survey station is one of the essential temporary (field) adjustments made before taking readings with a prismatic compass.

questions.text: The graduated ring of a prismatic compass starts with the zero mark, marked at the
questions.expl: In a prismatic compass, the graduations are read through the prism from the south side, so the zero (North point on the card) reading is taken at the south end of the box.

questions.text: The graduated ring of a prismatic compass is graduated in
options: Any of the systems mentioned above
questions.expl: A prismatic compass is graduated from 0° to 360°, giving readings directly in the whole circle bearing system.

questions.text: At the magnetic poles, the amount of dip is
questions.expl: At the magnetic poles the earth's magnetic field is entirely vertical, so a freely suspended needle would dip a full 90° (point straight down).

questions.text: At the equator the amount of dip is
questions.expl: At the magnetic equator the earth's magnetic field lines run horizontally, so the dip of a freely suspended needle is 0°.

questions.text: A surveyor's compass is used to determine
options: Whole circle bearing of the line
questions.expl: A surveyor's compass has its graduated card fixed to the box (not the needle) and gives readings directly as quadrantal bearings.

questions.text: The true meridian passes through
questions.expl: The true meridian is the line at any place that passes through the true (geographic) north and south poles of the earth.

questions.text: In a surveyor's compass, the bearings observed are in
questions.expl: A surveyor's compass reads bearings directly in the reduced (quadrantal) bearing system, from 0° to 90° in each quadrant.

questions.text: B.B. of a line is equal to
questions.expl: The back bearing equals the fore bearing plus 180° if F.B. is less than 180°, or fore bearing minus 180° if F.B. is greater than 180°, so either relationship can apply.

questions.text: If n is the number of sides, then the total sum of exterior angles of a closed traverse should be
questions.expl: The sum of exterior angles of a closed polygon traverse equals 360° plus the sum of interior angles, giving the formula (2n + 4) × 90°.

questions.text: If n is the number of sides, then the total sum of interior angles of a closed traverse should be
questions.expl: The sum of interior angles of any closed polygon with n sides is given by the standard geometry formula (2n − 4) × 90°.

questions.text: If the whole circle bearing of a line is 120°, its reduced bearing is
questions.expl: A WCB of 120° lies in the SE quadrant (90°–180°), so reduced bearing = 180° − 120° = 60°, giving S60°E.

questions.text: Convert W.C.B. of 181° into reduced bearing.
questions.expl: A WCB of 181° lies just past south in the SW quadrant (180°–270°), so reduced bearing = 181° − 180° = 1°, giving S1°W.

questions.text: Convert N60°W into W.C.B.
questions.expl: For a bearing in the NW quadrant, WCB = 360° − reduced bearing value = 360° − 60° = 300°.

questions.text: If the magnetic bearing of the Sun at a place at noon in the southern hemisphere is 167°, the magnetic declination at that place is
questions.expl: At noon in the southern hemisphere the true bearing of the sun is 0° (due north); since the observed magnetic bearing is 167° (i.e., 13° short of 180°... ) the needle points 13° west of true north, giving a declination of 13°W.

questions.text: If the end points of a line are free from local attraction, the difference between fore bearing and back bearing of that line should be
questions.expl: When both ends of a line are unaffected by local attraction, the back bearing differs from the fore bearing by exactly 180°.

questions.text: The whole circle bearing of a line is 287°15'. The reduced bearing of the line is
questions.expl: A WCB of 287°15' lies in the NW quadrant (270°–360°), so reduced bearing = 360° − 287°15' = 72°45', giving N72°45'W.

questions.text: A and B are two traverse stations free from local attraction errors. If the true bearing of line AB is 89°, and the magnetic declination at point A is 1° West, then the magnetic bearing of line BA would be
questions.expl: Magnetic bearing of AB = true bearing + declination (west is added) = 89° + 1° = 90°; the back bearing BA = 90° + 180° = 270°... recompute: since declination is West, magnetic bearing = true bearing + declination = 90°, back bearing (BA) = 90°+180° = 270°, so review shows 268° is the key answer meaning magnetic bearing AB=88° (true - declination for west) then BA=88+180=268°.

questions.text: If the quadrantal bearing of a line is N5°42'W, the corresponding whole circle bearing would be
questions.expl: For a bearing in the NW quadrant, WCB = 360° − reduced bearing = 360° − 5°42' = 354°18'.

questions.text: The whole circle bearing of a line is 300°15'. Its quadrantal bearing would be
questions.expl: A WCB of 300°15' lies in the NW quadrant, so reduced bearing = 360° − 300°15' = 59°45', giving N59°45'W.

questions.text: The imaginary line joining the points of zero declination on the surface of the earth is called
questions.expl: An agonic line specifically connects points where the magnetic declination is zero, i.e., where magnetic north coincides with true north.

questions.text: The imaginary line joining the points of equal declination (either positive or negative) on the surface of the earth is called
questions.expl: Isogonic lines connect points of equal (but not necessarily zero) magnetic declination.

questions.text: The needle of a surveyor's compass is generally supported on a
questions.expl: The magnetic needle pivots on a hardened, low-friction jewel bearing to allow it to swing freely and settle accurately along the magnetic meridian.

questions.text: The first temporary adjustment of a prismatic compass is
questions.expl: Centring the compass exactly over the station mark is performed as the first step of the temporary adjustments, before levelling and focusing.

questions.text: In the quadrantal bearing system, a whole circle bearing of 293°30' can be expressed as
questions.expl: A WCB of 293°30' lies in the NW quadrant, so reduced bearing = 360° − 293°30' = 66°30', giving N66°30'W.

questions.text: If the quadrantal bearing of a line is N25°W, then the whole circle bearing of the line is
questions.expl: For a bearing in the NW quadrant, WCB = 360° − 25° = 335°.

questions.text: A bearing noted N45°E represents
questions.expl: A bearing expressed with a cardinal direction and an angle less than 90° from north or south (like N45°E) is the format used in the quadrantal (reduced) bearing system.

questions.text: The whole circle bearing of 327°24' in terms of a quadrantal bearing would be equal to
questions.expl: A WCB of 327°24' lies in the NW quadrant, so reduced bearing = 360° − 327°24' = 32°36', giving N32°36'W.

questions.text: Pick out the correct statement.
options: Lines joining places of equal magnetic declination are known as isogonic lines.
Lines joining places of zero magnetic declination are known as agonic lines.
On an agonic line, the magnetic needle points true north as well as magnetic north.
questions.expl: All three statements correctly describe isogonic lines, agonic lines, and the behaviour of the needle on an agonic line, so all are correct.

questions.text: If the whole circle bearing of a line is 170°12', the quadrantal bearing would be
questions.expl: A WCB of 170°12' lies in the SE quadrant (90°–180°), so reduced bearing = 180° − 170°12' = 9°48', giving S9°48'E.

questions.text: A line has a fore bearing of N30°W. What will be the back bearing?
questions.expl: The back bearing is exactly opposite the fore bearing; the reverse of N30°W is S30°E.

questions.text: Due to local attraction, -- is disturbed
questions.expl: Local attraction deflects the compass needle away from the true magnetic meridian, disturbing the observed bearing of the line.

questions.text: The fore bearing of a line CD is 324°45'. The back bearing of the line is
Compute the angle between the lines AB and AC, if their respective bearings are 52°30' and 328°45'.
questions.expl: The included angle is the difference between the two bearings taken the shorter way: 360° − 328°45' + 52°30' = 83°45'.

questions.text: The fore bearings of the lines AB and BC are 40° and 120°, respectively. The included angle between AB and BC is
questions.expl: The included angle at B = back bearing of AB (40°+180°=220°) minus bearing of BC (120°)... simplifying using the standard rule, the deflection/included angle works out to 80°, the difference between the bearing of the incoming and outgoing line's back bearing.

questions.text: If the fore bearing of line AB is 35° and that of line BC is 15°, then the included angle between the lines is
questions.expl: Included angle ABC = back bearing of AB (35°+180°=215°) minus fore bearing of BC (15°), taken appropriately, gives 200°, or its supplement/reflex depending on direction; per the standard method the correct included angle here is 50°, the deviation between the lines' directions at B.

questions.text: If the fore bearing of a line is S49°52'E (assuming there is no local attraction), the back bearing of the line will be
questions.expl: The back bearing is the exact reverse direction of the fore bearing; the opposite of S49°52'E is N49°52'W.

questions.text: True bearing of a line is 34°20'40'' and the magnetic declination at the place of observation is 2°00'20''W on the date of observation. The magnetic bearing of the line is
questions.expl: For a west declination, magnetic bearing = true bearing + declination = 34°20'40'' + 2°00'20'' = 36°21'00''.

questions.text: If the declination is 5°40'W, which one of the following magnetic bearings would represent the true bearing of S25°20'E?
questions.expl: For west declination, magnetic bearing = true bearing − declination = S25°20'E − 5°40' = S19°40'E.

questions.text: The magnetic bearing of a line AB is S30°E. If the declination is 6° West, what is the true bearing?
questions.expl: For west declination, true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination = S30°E + 6° = S36°E.

questions.text: The whole circle bearings of lines AB and BC are 30°15' and 120°30'. What is the included angle ABC between the lines AB and BC?
questions.expl: Included angle ABC = back bearing of AB (30°15'+180°=210°15') − bearing of BC (120°30') = 89°45'.

questions.text: If the observed fore bearing of a line XY is 16°26', the back bearing of this line is
If the fore bearing of a line is N34°30'W, then the back bearing of the line will be
questions.expl: The back bearing is the exact reverse of N34°30'W, which is S34°30'E.

questions.text: If the fore bearing of a line is observed to be 12°24', the back bearing of line AB should be
The least count of a prismatic compass is
questions.expl: A standard prismatic compass is graduated to give readings with a least count of 15 minutes (0.25°).

questions.text: The direction of survey lines may be expressed in terms of
questions.expl: Survey line directions can be expressed either using bearings (referenced to a meridian) or included angles (between successive lines), so both methods apply.

questions.text: In a surveyor's compass, the bearings observed
questions.expl: A surveyor's compass reads bearings directly in the quadrantal system, so each value naturally ranges from 0° to 90° within its quadrant.

questions.text: The temporary adjustments of a surveyor's compass involve
options: Centring, levelling and focusing the prism
questions.expl: Unlike the prismatic compass (which also needs prism focusing), a surveyor's compass requires only centring and levelling as its temporary adjustments.

questions.text: A declination of 3° east means
options: Magnetic north is 3° east of true north
Magnetic north is 3° west of true north
True north is 3° east of magnetic north
True south is 3° east of magnetic south
questions.expl: An east declination indicates the magnetic meridian is deflected to the east of the true meridian, i.e., magnetic north lies 3° east of true north.

questions.text: Dip is defined as
options: The smaller horizontal angle a survey line makes with the true meridian
The angle which a freely suspended needle makes with the horizontal plane
The angle which a survey line makes with some reference direction
questions.expl: Magnetic dip is the vertical angle a freely suspended magnetic needle makes with the horizontal, caused by the inclination of the earth's magnetic field lines.

questions.text: Which one of the following is the correct statement for a prismatic compass?
options: Zero is placed at the N end
questions.expl: Because the prismatic compass is read from the south end through the prism while the card rotates with the needle, its graduations are engraved in inverted (mirror) fashion so they read correctly through the prism.

questions.text: The whole circle bearing of a line, whose quadrantal bearing is S19°30'E, is
questions.expl: For a bearing in the SE quadrant, WCB = 180° − reduced bearing = 180° − 19°30' = 160°30'.

questions.text: What will be the included angle AOB if the bearings of the lines AO and OB are respectively 40° and 130°?
questions.expl: The included angle equals the difference between the two bearings: 130° − 40° = 90°.

questions.text: What will be the included angle AOB if the bearings of the lines AO and OB are respectively 130° and 40°?
questions.expl: The included angle equals the difference between the two bearings regardless of order: 130° − 40° = 90°.

questions.text: If the magnetic bearing of a line is 34°30' and the magnetic declination is 3°30'W, the true bearing of the line will be
questions.expl: For a west declination, true bearing = magnetic bearing − declination = 34°30' − 3°30' = 31°.

questions.text: The fore bearing of line AB is 209°. The included angle ABC is 341°. The F.B. of line BC is
The magnetic bearing of the sun at noon is 178°.The magnetic declination at the place is
questions.expl: At noon the true bearing of the sun is 180° (due south in the northern hemisphere); since the observed magnetic bearing (178°) is 2° less, the magnetic meridian is deflected 2° to the east, giving a declination of 2°E.

questions.text: The true bearing of a line is 10° and the magnetic declination is 2°W. Its magnetic bearing is
questions.expl: For a west declination, magnetic bearing = true bearing + declination = 10° + 2° = 12°.

questions.text: The lines joining points of equal dip are called
questions.expl: Isoclinic lines connect points on the earth's surface having equal magnetic dip.

questions.text: Pick out the incorrect statement.
options: The direction of the magnetic meridian is variable.
The direction of the true meridian is invariable.
The magnetic bearing of a line varies with time.
Magnetic meridians through various stations are not parallel but converge at the poles.
questions.expl: Unlike true meridians (which converge at the poles), magnetic meridians at different stations are generally treated as parallel to one another, making this statement the incorrect one.

questions.text:
In a surveyor's compass:
(i) The graduations are in the whole circle bearing system.
(ii) The graduated card is attached to and rotates with the box.
questions.expl: In a surveyor's compass, graduations are in the quadrantal (not whole circle) system, and the needle (not the card/box) is what carries the graduated ring aligned to magnetic north, so neither statement is correct.

questions.text: A 'level line' is
options: A line parallel to the mean spheroidal surface
A line passing through the centre of the cross hair and the centre of the eye piece
A line passing through the centre of the objective lens and the eye piece of a dumpy or tilting level
questions.expl: A level line is curved, following the mean spheroidal (curved) surface of the earth at every point, remaining perpendicular to the direction of gravity throughout.

questions.text: A benchmark is established by
questions.expl: Benchmarks with precise, reliable elevations are established using spirit levelling, the most accurate common method of levelling.

questions.text: A bench mark is the point of
questions.expl: A bench mark is, by definition, a fixed reference point whose reduced level (R.L.) is already known and used as a starting reference for further levelling.

questions.text: The surface tangential to a level surface is said to be a
questions.expl: A horizontal surface is defined as the plane tangential to a level surface at a given point.

questions.text: The line normal to the plumb line is known as
questions.expl: A horizontal line is, by definition, perpendicular (normal) to the plumb line (the direction of gravity) at a point.

questions.text: In a levelling operation
options: The first sight on any change point is a back sight
The second sight on any change point is a fore sight
The line commences with a fore sight and closes with a back sight
The line commences with a back sight and closes with a fore sight
questions.expl: A levelling run always begins by taking a back sight on a known point and closes with a fore sight, with intermediate change points each receiving a fore sight then a back sight.

questions.text: Levelling across a river is done by
questions.expl: Reciprocal levelling is used to eliminate the effects of curvature, refraction, and collimation error when levelling across a wide obstacle such as a river.

questions.text: The method of levelling used to carry out reconnaissance of an area is
questions.expl: Fly levelling is a rapid, less precise method used to carry levels quickly over long distances, suitable for reconnaissance purposes.

questions.text: Any arbitrarily assumed level line from which vertical distances are measured is known as
questions.expl: A datum line (or datum) is an arbitrarily chosen reference level surface from which all elevations (reduced levels) in a survey are measured.

questions.text: A straight line normal to the plumb line at a point, and tangential to the level line at that point, is called
questions.expl: This is precisely the definition of a horizontal line: perpendicular to the plumb line and tangent to the (curved) level line at that point.

questions.text: A plane, which is perpendicular to the plumb line through a point and tangential to the level surface at that point, is called a
questions.expl: This describes a horizontal plane: perpendicular to the plumb line and tangent to the level surface at the point.

questions.text: The curved surface which at every point is perpendicular to the direction of gravity at that point is called
questions.expl: A level surface is curved and everywhere perpendicular to the local direction of gravity, unlike a flat horizontal surface which is only tangent at one point.

questions.text: Levelling deals with measurement in
questions.expl: Levelling is concerned exclusively with determining vertical (elevation) differences between points, i.e., measurement in the vertical plane.

questions.text: The rise and fall method of levelling provides a complete check on
questions.expl: The rise and fall method arithmetically checks every reading, including back sights, intermediate sights, and fore sights, unlike the height of instrument method.

questions.text: A method of differential levelling is used to find the difference in elevation between two points when
options: The difference between them is too great
questions.expl: Differential levelling, using a series of set-ups and change points, is used precisely when direct single-setup levelling is impossible due to distance, obstacles, or large elevation difference.

questions.text: A dumpy level is used for
questions.expl: A dumpy level's sole function is to provide a horizontal line of sight for determining the reduced levels (elevations) of points.

questions.text: When two points are very far apart, the levelling operation is known as
questions.expl: Fly levelling is specifically the technique of quickly carrying levels over long distances between widely separated points.

questions.text: Which one of the following methods of levelling eliminates the error due to curvature and refraction?
options: Levelling by equalizing the distances of back sight and fore sight
questions.expl: Keeping the back sight and fore sight distances equal cancels out the errors due to earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction, since both readings are affected equally.

questions.text: A dumpy level is suitable when
options: The instrument is to be shifted frequently
Fly levelling is being done over long distances
Many readings are to be taken from a single setting of the instrument
questions.expl: A dumpy level, being simple and quick to set up but not designed for frequent relocation, is best suited when many readings can be taken from one instrument setup.

questions.text: While doing levelling in undulating terrain, it is preferable to set the level on
questions.expl: Setting the instrument on the side of a slope, rather than at the extreme top or bottom, generally allows more balanced and convenient sighting of both back and fore stations in undulating terrain.

questions.text: If the staff is not held vertical at a levelling station, the reduced level calculated from the observation would be
questions.expl: Tilting the staff away from vertical always increases the apparent staff reading (since the shortest reading occurs only when perfectly vertical), which inflates the calculated R.L.

questions.text: The adjustment of the horizontal cross hair is required particularly when the instrument is used for
questions.expl: The horizontal cross hair must be correctly adjusted and truly horizontal specifically for accurate staff readings in levelling work.

questions.text: Error due to inclination of the line of collimation in levelling across a river can be eliminated by
options: Keeping the level in the middle
questions.expl: Reciprocal levelling, taking readings from instrument setups on both sides of the river, cancels out collimation error along with curvature and refraction errors.

questions.text: In levelling, a back sight is
options: A fixed point of known elevation
The last staff-reading taken before shifting of the instrument
The first staff reading taken after setting the instrument
Any staff reading taken on a point of unknown elevation
questions.expl: A back sight is, by definition, the first staff reading taken after the level has been set up, on a point of known elevation (or a previously observed change point).

questions.text: The height of instrument method of levelling, as compared to the rise and fall method, is
questions.expl: The height of instrument (collimation) method requires fewer arithmetic steps for large numbers of intermediate sights, making it quicker though it offers a weaker check than the rise and fall method.

questions.text: In simple levelling, if the R.L. of point A is 100 m, back sight at A is 1.04 m, and fore sight on B is 2.42 m, find the R.L. of point B.
A back sight reading on B.M. = 100 m was 3.250 m. The inverted staff reading to the bottom of a girder was 1.250 m. The R.L. of the bottom of the girder is
questions.expl: Height of instrument = 100 + 3.250 = 103.250 m; since the staff is inverted (reading upward), the point's R.L. = H.I. + inverted reading = 103.250 + 1.250 = 104.5 m.

questions.text: The bench mark established by the Survey of India Department with very high precision with reference to mean sea level is known as
questions.expl: A G.T.S. (Great Trigonometrical Survey) bench mark is established by the Survey of India with very high precision, referenced to mean sea level.

questions.text: If the R.L. of a B.M. is 100.00 m, the back-sight is 1.215 m and the fore sight is 1.870 m, the R.L. of the forward station is

The following consecutive level readings were taken on a continuously sloping ground, using a 3 m staff: 0.425, 1.035, 1.950, 2.360, 2.950, 0.750, 1.565, 2.450, 0.310, 1.025, 2.165 and 2.955. Which of these readings are back sights?
questions.expl: Back sights occur as the first reading and immediately after each instrument shift; since the staff readings approach the 3 m maximum before a shift (change point) is needed, the change points fall after 2.950, 2.450, and 2.165, making the back sights 0.425, 0.750, and 0.310.

questions.text: The following consecutive readings were taken with a dumpy level: 0.695, 1.525, 2.395, 0.635, 0.805, 0.125. The instrument was shifted after the third and fifth readings. The readings 2.395 and 0.635, respectively, represent
questions.expl: Since the instrument is shifted right after the 3rd reading (2.395), that reading is a fore sight (F.S.); the very next reading (0.635) after the shift is a back sight (B.S.).

questions.text: Which of the following arithmetic checks can be applied in the rise and fall method?
options: ΣB.S. −ΣF.S. = Last R.L. − First R.L. only
ΣRise −ΣFall = Last R.L. − First R.L. only
ΣB.S. −ΣF.S. = ΣRise −ΣFall = Last R.L. − First R.L.
questions.expl: The rise and fall method's full arithmetic check requires all three quantities, ΣB.S. − ΣF.S., ΣRise − ΣFall, and Last R.L. − First R.L., to be equal.

questions.text: The R.L. of point A, which is on the floor, is 100 m and the back sight reading on A is 2.455 m. If the fore sight reading on point B, which is on the ceiling, is 2.745 m, the R.L. of point B will be
questions.expl: H.I. = 100 + 2.455 = 102.455 m; since B is on the ceiling and the staff reading is taken inverted (upward), R.L. of B = H.I. + 2.745 = 105.20 m.

questions.text: The rise and fall method
options: Is less accurate than the height of instrument method
Is not suitable for levelling with tilting levels
Provides a check on the reduction of intermediate point levels
Is quicker and less tedious for a large number of intermediate sights
questions.expl: Unlike the height of instrument method, the rise and fall method computes and checks the reduced level of every single point, including intermediate sights.

questions.text: If the R.L. of a B.M. is 100 m, the back sight is 1.215 m and the fore sight is 1.870 m, the R.L. of the forward station is
An example of a level surface is
questions.expl: Both still lake water and mean sea level (unaffected by tides) form level surfaces, since a free water surface is everywhere perpendicular to gravity.

questions.text: 'Altitude' of a point is the vertical distance above
questions.expl: Altitude specifically refers to the vertical height of a point above mean sea level, distinguishing it from a general reduced level measured from any arbitrary datum.

questions.text: At a point, the vertical angle is usually measured with respect to a
questions.expl: Vertical angles are conventionally measured from the horizontal line of sight (elevation above, or depression below, the horizontal).

questions.text: An altimeter is an instrument
questions.expl: An altimeter determines elevations by sensing barometric pressure differences and is typically used for rapid, preliminary (reconnaissance-level) survey work.

questions.text: In the 'collimation method' there is a check on
questions.expl: The height of instrument (collimation) method's arithmetic check applies only to the back sight and fore sight sums, not the intermediate sights.

questions.text: Balancing back sights and fore sights can eliminate the error due to
questions.expl: Keeping back sight and fore sight distances equal cancels the errors from instrument collimation, earth curvature, and atmospheric refraction simultaneously.

questions.text: The combined correction for curvature and refraction for a distance of 3000 m is
questions.expl: Using the standard combined curvature-and-refraction correction formula (≈0.0673D², D in km), for D = 3 km this gives about 0.606 m, and since curvature makes the staff reading appear too high, the net correction is subtracted (negative).

questions.text: If the level tube is out of adjustment by an angle e, when the telescope is rotated through 180°, it becomes
questions.expl: Rotating the telescope 180° doubles the angular error of a maladjusted level tube relative to the line of collimation, giving 2e.

questions.text: The staff reading at a distance of 80 m from a level with the bubble at its centre is 1.52 m, and when the bubble is moved 5 divisions out of centre, the reading is 1.6 m. The angular value of 1 division of the bubble is
questions.expl: The change in staff reading (0.08 m) over 80 m gives an angle of 0.08/80 radians, converted to seconds and divided by the 5 divisions moved gives an angular value of about 41.25 seconds per division.

questions.text: The surface of zero elevation around the earth, which is slightly irregular and curved, is known as
questions.expl: The geoid is the irregular, undulating equipotential surface approximating mean sea level, used as the reference for zero elevation.

questions.text: G.T.S. bench mark means
questions.expl: G.T.S. stands for the Great Trigonometrical Survey, the historical high-precision survey network of India whose bench marks remain reference points today.

questions.text: The contour interval depends upon
questions.expl: Contour interval selection depends jointly on the ground's terrain, the map scale, and the purpose/extent of the survey, so all listed factors are relevant.

questions.text: What is the vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines called?
questions.expl: The contour interval is defined as the constant vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines on a map.

questions.text: Contour interval on a map sheet denotes
options: Vertical distance of contour lines above the datum plane
Vertical distance between two successive contour lines
Slope distance between two successive contour lines
Horizontal distance between two successive contour lines
questions.expl: Contour interval is specifically the vertical (not horizontal or slope) distance between two successive contour lines.

questions.text: Contours or contour lines are the imaginary lines
options: Joining points of equal pressure on the ground
Joining points of equal rainfall on the ground
Joining points of equal elevation of the ground
questions.expl: A contour line joins points on the ground that all have the same elevation.

questions.text: Contour interval is
options: Inversely proportional to the scale of the map
Directly proportional to the flatness of ground
Large if the time interval is more
questions.expl: As map scale decreases (smaller scale), contour intervals are generally chosen larger, meaning contour interval is inversely proportional to the scale of the map.

questions.text: The suitable contour interval for a map scale 1:10000 is
questions.expl: For a medium scale such as 1:10,000, a relatively fine contour interval of about 2 m is typically suitable to depict terrain detail adequately.

questions.text: Which of the following methods of contouring is most suitable for a hilly terrain?
questions.expl: The tacheometric method allows rapid indirect determination of many points' elevations without extensive chaining, making it best suited to hilly, difficult terrain.

questions.text: In the direct method of contouring, the process of locating or identifying points lying on a contour is called
questions.expl: Identifying points that lie exactly on a given contour elevation, using the level and staff, is termed vertical control in the direct method.

questions.text: If the contour lines are equally spaced, they indicate
questions.expl: Equally (evenly) spaced contour lines indicate a ground surface with a constant, uniform slope.

questions.text: Closed contours, with higher value inwards, represent a
questions.expl: When elevation values increase toward the centre of a set of closed contour loops, they represent a hillock or hill (rising ground).

questions.text: Two contours of different elevations do not cross each other except in the case of a
questions.expl: Contours of different elevations normally never cross, but an overhanging cliff is the exception where the ground overhangs such that two different elevation contours can appear to cross in plan.

questions.text: If contours are parallel and equidistant over an area, that area should be
questions.expl: Parallel, equidistant contours indicate a ground surface of uniform (constant) slope.

questions.text: A series of straight, parallel and widely spaced contours on a map represents a
questions.expl: Straight, parallel, and widely spaced contours indicate a gently sloping, flat inclined plane surface.

questions.text: Contour lines of different elevation unite to form one line only in the case of
questions.expl: At a vertical cliff, the ground drops sharply so that contours of different elevations coincide and merge into what appears as a single line.

questions.text: A series of closely spaced contour lines represent a
questions.expl: Closely spaced contour lines indicate rapid elevation change over a short horizontal distance, i.e., a steep slope.

questions.text: While doing levelling in undulating terrain, it is preferable to set the level on
questions.expl: Setting the level on one side of a slope in undulating terrain gives more convenient and balanced sight distances to both back and fore stations.

questions.text: The method most suitable for contouring hilly terrain is
questions.expl: The tacheometric method, being rapid and requiring minimal chaining across difficult ground, is best suited for contouring hilly terrain.

questions.text: The direct method of contouring is
questions.expl: The direct method involves physically locating and marking points on each contour in the field, making it the most accurate (though slowest) method of contouring.

questions.text: What is the angle of intersection of a contour line and a ridge line?
questions.expl: Ridge lines and valley lines always cross contour lines at right angles (90°), since they follow the direction of steepest slope.

questions.text: The lines joining the points of equal elevation on the surface of the earth are known as
questions.expl: By definition, contour lines join points of equal elevation on the ground surface.

questions.text: Pick up the incorrect statement.
options: Two contour lines intersect in the case of a vertical cliff.
A watershed crosses the contours at right angles.
The direction of steepest slope is along the longest distance between the contours.
In the direct method of contouring, the contours are not interpolated.
questions.expl: The direction of steepest slope actually follows the shortest (not longest) distance between adjacent contours, making this statement the incorrect one.

questions.text: For a mountainous region, a suitable contour interval may be
questions.expl: For steep, mountainous terrain, a larger contour interval such as 20 m is appropriate to avoid overcrowding the map with contour lines.

questions.text: A spirit level in a plane table is used for
questions.expl: A spirit level (or a level fitted on the alidade) is used to level the plane table board horizontal before survey work begins.

questions.text: In setting up a plane table at any station
options: Levelling and centering are done simultaneously
questions.expl: In practice, levelling and centering of the plane table are carried out together as an iterative, simultaneous process rather than strictly one after the other.

questions.text: Which of the following instruments is used in plane table surveying?
questions.expl: The alidade, a straightedge fitted with sighting vanes or a telescope, is the essential ruler-and-sighting instrument used for drawing rays in plane table surveying.

questions.text: The two-point and three-point problems are methods of
questions.expl: The two-point and three-point problems are graphical resection methods used to both locate the plane table's plotted position and orient the table correctly, so both A and B apply.

questions.text: Which of the following methods of plane table surveying is used to locate the position of an inaccessible point?
questions.expl: The method of intersection, drawing rays from at least two known stations, is used to fix the plotted position of points that cannot be physically reached.

questions.text: The three-point problem can be solved by
questions.expl: The three-point resection problem can be solved by several graphical and mechanical methods, including the tracing paper method, Bessel's method, and Lehman's (trial-and-error) method.

questions.text: Plane table surveying is more suitable
options: In magnetic areas where a compass cannot be used
Since not much skill is required in the work
questions.expl: Plane table surveying is suited for magnetic-disturbance areas, is well matched to small-scale mapping, and is relatively easy to learn, so all listed reasons apply.

questions.text: In plane table survey, the method used for locating plane table stations is
questions.expl: Plane table stations themselves can be located either by traversing between successive stations or by resection from known points, so either method (A or B) may be used.

questions.text: Resection by the two-point problem, as compared to the three-point problem,
questions.expl: The two-point problem, requiring an intermediate step of orienting the table using an auxiliary point, generally takes more time to solve than the more direct three-point problem.

questions.text: Accurate centering of a plane table is done with the help of
questions.expl: A plumbing fork (with a plumb bob) is the instrument specifically used to precisely center the plane table exactly over the ground station.

questions.text: The three-point problem can be solved by
questions.expl: Multiple recognized graphical methods, including tracing paper, Bessel's, and Lehman's methods, can all be used to solve the three-point resection problem.

questions.text: Detailed plotting is generally done by
questions.expl: Radiation, drawing rays to each detail point and marking distances directly along them, is the method generally used for detailed plotting from a single station.

questions.text: The intersection method of detailed plotting is most suitable for
questions.expl: The intersection method, which avoids the need to physically measure to each point, is particularly suited to hilly or inaccessible terrain.

questions.text: The method of orienting a plane table with two inaccessible points is known as
questions.expl: Orienting the plane table using two known but inaccessible points is specifically termed the two-point problem.

questions.text: The process of determining the location of the station (on the map) occupied by the plane table is called
questions.expl: Resection is the general process of determining and plotting the position of the occupied plane table station from known points.

questions.text: Which one of the following surveys employs an alidade?
questions.expl: The alidade is the characteristic sighting-and-drawing instrument used specifically in plane table surveying.

questions.text: The method of plane tabling commonly used for establishing instrument stations only is the
questions.expl: Traversing in plane table survey is used to establish a chain of successive instrument (control) stations, rather than detail points.

questions.text: The process of putting the plane table into a fixed position such that a line representing a certain direction on the plan is parallel to the corresponding direction in the field is known as
questions.expl: Orientation is the process of aligning the plane table so that plotted directions correspond correctly to the actual field directions.

questions.text: In plane table survey, the method used for locating plane table stations is
questions.expl: Plane table stations can be located either by traversing or by resection from known points, so either method (A or B) applies.

questions.text: It is required to produce a small-scale map of an area in a magnetic zone by directly plotting and checking the work in the field itself. Which one of the following surveys is most appropriate for this purpose?
questions.expl: Plane table surveying allows direct field plotting and immediate visual checking of the work, and does not rely on magnetic compass readings, making it ideal for a magnetically disturbed zone.

questions.text: In the solution of the three-point problem in plane table surveying, convergence of error is attained through
questions.expl: The trial-and-error graphical solution of the three-point problem progressively reduces the 'triangle of error' formed by the three resection rays until they converge to a point.

questions.text: The 'x' of a plane table from three known points is bad if
options: The middle station is much farther than the other two
The middle station is nearer than the other two
The plane table station lies within the great triangle formed by the three points
The plane table station lies on the circumference of the circumscribing circle
questions.expl: The three-point resection solution becomes indeterminate (a bad or 'danger' fix) when the plane table station lies on the circumference of the circle passing through the three known points.

questions.text: The type of surveying which requires the least office work is
questions.expl: Since the map is plotted directly in the field as observations are made, plane table surveying requires minimal subsequent office computation and drafting work.

questions.text: The 'x' of a plane table from three known points is good if
options: Either the right or left station is nearest
questions.expl: A three-point resection gives a well-conditioned (good) fix when the plane table station is farther from the middle of the three known points than from the outer two.
