2. At least two rays are drawn from two different stations to the detail to be located
3. Rays are drawn in the direction of details through the station point on which the table is set up
4. Rays are drawn on the map by setting up the table over each of the stations towards the subsequent station
questions.expl: Traversing sets up over each station in sequence sighting the next (procedure 4); resection locates the occupied station itself (procedure 1); intersection uses rays from two stations to a detail (procedure 2); radiation draws rays through the occupied station toward details (procedure 3), giving A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3.

questions.text: If every one of the three angles of a triangle has a probable error of ±1'', what will be the probable error in the sum of the so-measured internal angles of the triangle?
questions.expl: Errors combine as the square root of the sum of squares of independent errors: √(1²+1²+1²) = √3, giving a probable error of ±√3'' in the total angle sum.

questions.text: In a plane-table survey, the process of determining the plotted position of a station occupied by the plane table, by means of sights taken towards known points already plotted, is known as
questions.expl: This is precisely the definition of resection: fixing the plotted position of the occupying station by sighting toward known, already-plotted points.

questions.text: The plotting of inaccessible points in a plane-table survey can be done by the method of
questions.expl: Intersection allows the position of a point to be plotted purely from rays drawn from two known stations, without needing to reach or measure directly to the point, so it is used for inaccessible points.

questions.text: A theodolite is an instrument used for measurement of
questions.expl: A theodolite is designed to precisely measure both horizontal and vertical angles, distinguishing it from simpler instruments limited to one type of angle.

questions.text: The imaginary line passing through the intersection of the cross hairs and the optical centre of the objective glass, and its continuation, is known as
questions.expl: This is precisely the definition of the line of collimation, the fundamental reference line of a surveying telescope.

questions.text: In an adjusted level, when the bubble is centered, the axis of the bubble tube becomes parallel to the
questions.expl: When properly adjusted and the bubble is centred, the axis of the bubble tube becomes parallel to the line of collimation, ensuring a truly horizontal line of sight.

questions.text: In a theodolite, a condition arising when the image formed by the objective is not in the plane of the cross hairs is known as
questions.expl: Parallax occurs when the image and the cross hairs are not in the same focal plane, causing apparent relative movement between them as the observer's eye shifts.

questions.text: Cross hairs in surveying telescopes are fitted
options: At the centre of the telescope
At the optical centre of the eye piece
questions.expl: Cross hairs are mounted on a diaphragm located near the eyepiece end of the telescope, at its focal plane.

questions.text: Setting out a simple curve by the two-theodolite method does not require
questions.expl: The two-theodolite method relies purely on angular intersection from two stations, so linear (chain/tape) measurements are not required.

questions.text: In an internal focusing type of telescope, the lens provided is
questions.expl: An internal focusing telescope uses an additional movable concave lens between the objective and the diaphragm to focus the image.

questions.text: The cross hairs in a surveying telescope are placed
options: Midway between the eye-piece and objective lens
Much closer to the eye-piece than to the objective lens
Much closer to the objective lens than to the eyepiece
Anywhere between the eye-piece and objective lens
questions.expl: Cross hairs are positioned on a diaphragm much closer to the eyepiece than to the objective lens, at the eyepiece's focal plane.

questions.text: A telescope is said to be inverted if its
options: Vertical circle is to its right and the bubble of the telescope is down
Vertical circle is to its right and the bubble of the telescope is up
Vertical circle is to its left and the bubble of the telescope is down
Vertical circle is to its left and the bubble of the telescope is up
questions.expl: A telescope is described as 'inverted' or 'face right' when the vertical circle is to the observer's right and the telescope bubble is underneath (down).

questions.text: Size of a theodolite is specified by
options: The diameter of the vertical circle
The diameter of the lower plate
The diameter of the upper plate
questions.expl: By convention, the nominal size of a theodolite is specified by the diameter of its lower (graduated horizontal) plate.

questions.text: The process of turning the telescope about the vertical axis in a horizontal plane is known as
questions.expl: Rotating the telescope about the vertical axis, sweeping through the horizontal plane, is called swinging.

questions.text: In a transit theodolite, error due to eccentricity of verniers is eliminated by reading
options: Both right swing and left swing
Different parts of the main scale
questions.expl: Reading both verniers (on opposite sides of the circle) and taking the mean cancels out the error introduced by eccentricity between the circle's centre and the vernier arm's pivot.

questions.text: When taking a back sight with a theodolite, the screw which is tightened first is the
questions.expl: To take a back sight, the lower clamp screw is engaged first to fix the horizontal circle, allowing later readings for the fore sight to be measured relative to it using the upper motion.

questions.text: The process of turning the telescope about the horizontal axis in a vertical plane by a 180° revolution is known as
questions.expl: This 180° flip of the telescope about the horizontal axis is referred to interchangeably as reversing, transiting, or plunging in surveying terminology.

questions.text: The size of a theodolite is defined by
options: The diameter of the graduated circle of the lower plate
The diameter of the graduated circle of the upper plate
questions.expl: A theodolite's nominal size is defined by the diameter of the graduated circle on its lower plate.

questions.text: The operation consisting of revolving the telescope through 180° in a vertical plane about its horizontal axis is called
questions.expl: This 180° revolution of the telescope about the horizontal axis is termed transiting (also known as plunging or reversing).

questions.text: A theodolite is an instrument used for
questions.expl: A theodolite can measure horizontal angles, vertical angles, and (by observing bearings relative to a known meridian) bearings, so all listed uses apply.

questions.text: A telescope is said to be normal or direct if its
options: Vertical circle is to the left of the observer and the bubble is up
Vertical circle is to the left of the observer and the bubble is down
Vertical circle is to the right of the observer and the bubble is down
Vertical circle is to the right of the observer and the bubble is up
questions.expl: The telescope is in the 'normal' or 'direct' (face left) position when its vertical circle is to the observer's right and the telescope bubble is on top (up).

questions.text: The process of establishing intermediate points with the help of a theodolite on a given straight line whose ends are not intervisible is called
questions.expl: Establishing intermediate points on a straight line using a theodolite, especially when the end stations are not intervisible, is termed 'lining in.'

questions.text: The process of establishing intermediate points on a given straight line is called
questions.expl: Fixing intermediate points on a straight line is generally referred to as lining in.

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the levelling head?
options: To support the main part of the instrument
To attach the theodolite to the tripod
To provide a means for levelling the theodolite
questions.expl: The levelling head supports the theodolite's upper parts, attaches the instrument to the tripod, and provides the mechanism (foot screws) for levelling, so all listed functions apply.

questions.text: Removal of parallax may be achieved by
options: Refocusing the eyepiece and the objective
questions.expl: Eliminating parallax requires focusing both the eyepiece (on the cross hairs) and the objective (on the target image), so both must be refocused.

questions.text: For which of the following permanent adjustments of a theodolite is the spire test used?
options: Adjustment of altitude bubble and vertical index frame
questions.expl: The spire test checks and adjusts the horizontal (trunnion) axis of a theodolite by sighting a high point and verifying it can be re-observed identically in both faces.

questions.text: Pick up the correct statement.
options: Spire test is the name of the collimation-in-azimuth test.
During transiting, the wing nuts of the theodolite are loosened.
Poor focusing of a theodolite results in an instrumental error.
A deflection angle is that which a survey line makes with the prolongation of the preceding line.
questions.expl: During transiting (plunging the telescope through 180°), the relevant wing nuts/clamp screws must be loosened to permit the telescope to rotate freely about the horizontal axis.

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The axis of the plate level should be parallel to the vertical axis.
The axis of the striding level must be parallel to the horizontal axis.
The axis of the altitude level must be perpendicular to the line of collimation.
The line of collimation must be perpendicular to the plate level axis.
questions.expl: One of the fundamental permanent adjustments of a theodolite requires the axis of the striding level to be exactly parallel to the horizontal (trunnion) axis.

questions.text: Which of the following methods of contouring is most suitable for hilly terrain?
questions.expl: The tacheometric method allows quick, indirect determination of elevations without extensive chaining, making it best suited for hilly terrain.

questions.text: The branch of surveying in which measurement of distances is done by computation is known as
questions.expl: Tacheometric surveying determines horizontal and vertical distances indirectly through computation from stadia readings rather than direct chaining.

questions.text: Tacheometric survey is particularly adopted where
options: Obstacles, steep and broken ground, deep ravines, etc. exist
Too many curves at the border exist
Measurement of bodies of water are involved
questions.expl: Tacheometry is especially valuable where direct chaining is difficult or impossible, such as across obstacles, steep or broken ground, and deep ravines.

questions.text: The tacheometric method is more suitable for preparing the contour map of
questions.expl: Tacheometry's rapid indirect distance and elevation determination makes it most suitable for contouring hilly ground.

questions.text: The subtense tacheometry method is adopted when the ground is
questions.expl: Subtense bar tacheometry, which assumes horizontal sights of fixed intercept, is best suited for relatively flat ground conditions.

questions.text: An anallatic lens is provided in a
questions.expl: An anallatic lens is a special additional convex lens fitted in a tacheometer's telescope to eliminate the additive constant of the stadia formula.

questions.text: The multiplying constant of a tacheometer is
questions.expl: The multiplying constant in the stadia formula is given by the ratio of the focal length to the stadia hair spacing, f/i.

questions.text: The additive constant of a tacheometer is
questions.expl: The additive constant of the stadia formula is the sum of the focal length and the distance from the objective lens to the trunnion axis, f + d.

questions.text: For a tacheometer, the additive and multiplying constants are respectively
questions.expl: With an anallatic lens fitted, the additive constant is reduced to 0, while the multiplying constant is conventionally kept at the standard value of 100.

questions.text: Under favourable conditions, the error in tacheometric surveying will be less than
questions.expl: Under good conditions, tacheometric distance measurement can achieve an accuracy better than 1 in 1000.

questions.text: While making measurements in tacheometric surveying, the corrections will be of
questions.expl: Since tacheometric distances are computed from stadia readings rather than direct taping, the usual slope and tension (pull) corrections applicable to chaining do not apply.

questions.text: An anallatic lens is
questions.expl: The anallatic lens fitted in a tacheometer's telescope is an additional convex lens placed between the objective and the eyepiece.

questions.text: The method generally preferred for contouring rough country, where ordinary levelling is tedious and chaining is slow and inaccurate, is
questions.expl: Tacheometric surveying is preferred in rough terrain precisely because it avoids the slow, difficult chaining and levelling required by conventional methods.

questions.text: If only a horizontal cross-wire is/are provided in the stadia diaphragm of a tacheometer, these may be
questions.expl: A stadia diaphragm typically has two horizontal stadia hairs (in addition to the central cross hair) used to measure the staff intercept.

questions.text: The diaphragm of a stadia theodolite is normally fitted with two additional
questions.expl: A stadia diaphragm carries two additional horizontal stadia hairs, above and below the main horizontal cross hair, used to read the staff intercept.

questions.text:
Which of the following represents a correct match?
(i) Movable hair method: the intercept on the staff is kept constant and the stadia hair interval is variable.
(ii) Fixed hair method: the intercept on the staff is variable and the stadia hair interval is fixed.
(iii) Tangential method: the stadia hairs are not used.
options: None of the above is correct
questions.expl: All three descriptions correctly characterize the movable hair, fixed hair, and tangential tacheometric methods respectively.

questions.text: The stadia method in tacheometry is used to determine
questions.expl: The stadia method computes both the horizontal distance to the staff and the elevation difference (vertical distance) simultaneously from the stadia readings and vertical angle.

questions.text: The purpose of an anallatic lens in a tacheometer is to
options: Reduce the effective length of the telescope
Make the staff intercept proportional to its distance from the tacheometer
questions.expl: An anallatic lens fixes the geometry so that the staff intercept is always exactly proportional to the horizontal distance, eliminating the additive constant from the distance equation.

questions.text: The multiplying constant of a tacheometer is generally about
questions.expl: Manufacturers standardize the multiplying constant f/i to be 100 for convenience in tacheometric calculations.

questions.text: A subtense bar can be used to determine
options: Long distances of up to a km
Short distances of up to 200 m
Very short distances of up to a few centimetres
Very long distances of up to 100 km
questions.expl: A subtense bar, being of limited fixed length, is practically effective only for relatively short distances, typically up to about 200 m.

questions.text: If a staff is held normal to the line of sight and the angles of elevation and depression are kept the same, then the horizontal distance between the instrument station and the staff station computed by observations will be
options: Greater at an angle of elevation than at an angle of depression
Greater at an angle of depression than at an angle of elevation
questions.expl: With the staff normal to the line of sight, the horizontal distance formula depends symmetrically (through cos²θ) on the magnitude of the vertical angle, giving the same computed horizontal distance whether that angle is one of elevation or depression.

questions.text: If the focal length of an object glass is 25 cm, the stadia interval is 1.25 mm, and the distance from the object glass to the trunnion axis is 15 cm, the additive constant (in m) is
questions.expl: Additive constant = f + d = 0.25 m + 0.15 m = 0.40 m.

questions.text: In tangential tacheometry, an ordinary level staff is used which
options: Leans towards the instrument for an inclined sight upward
Leans away from the instrument for an inclined sight downward
Is equipped with two targets a fixed distance apart
questions.expl: In tangential tacheometry an ordinary level staff fitted with two targets set a fixed known distance apart is used, with two vertical angles observed to each target.

questions.text: If the vertical angles of inclined sights do not exceed 10° and the non-verticality of the staff remains within 1°, the stadia system of tacheometric observation can be made with
options: Staff normal as well as vertical
questions.expl: For small vertical angles (up to 10°) and slight staff tilt (within 1°), the resulting error is negligible, so the staff can be held either normal or vertical with acceptable accuracy.

questions.text: The intercept on a staff
options: Is maximum, if the staff is held truly normal to the line of sight
Is minimum, if the staff is held truly normal to the line of sight
Decreases, if the staff is tilted away from normal
Decreases, if the staff is tilted towards normal
questions.expl: The staff intercept is at its maximum value when the staff is held exactly perpendicular (normal) to the line of sight; any tilt away from normal reduces the intercept.

questions.text: Pick out the incorrect statement.
options: Tacheometry is preferred over chaining on undulating grounds.
Tacheometry is very suitable for preliminary location surveys.
Vertical holding of staves is better than normal holding, since the error on account of improper staff holding is less.
A subtense hair is used to measure short distances.
questions.expl: In fact, normal holding of the staff (perpendicular to the line of sight) reduces the error caused by imperfect staff holding compared to vertical holding, making this statement the incorrect one.

questions.text: Horizontal distances obtained by tacheometric observations
options: Do not require slope and pull correction
questions.expl: Since tacheometric distance is computed directly (accounting for the vertical angle already) from stadia readings rather than by taping along the slope, the usual chaining corrections for slope and pull do not apply.

questions.text: Horizontal cross-wires provided in the stadia diaphragm of a tacheometer may be
questions.expl: A stadia diaphragm carries two horizontal stadia cross-wires, positioned symmetrically above and below the main horizontal hair.

questions.text: If the spacing of cross-hairs in a stadia diaphragm of a tacheometer is 12 mm, and the focal length of the object glass is 24 cm, then the multiplying constant of the tacheometer is
questions.expl: Multiplying constant = f/i = 240 mm / 12 mm = 20.

questions.text: If a staff is held normal to the line of sight and the angles of elevation and depression are kept the same, then the horizontal distance between instrument station and staff station computed by observations will be
options: Greater at an angle of elevation than at an angle of depression
Greater at an angle of depression than at an angle of elevation
questions.expl: With the staff normal to the line of sight in both cases, the horizontal distance formula depends symmetrically on the vertical angle, giving the same computed horizontal distance for equal elevation and depression angles.

questions.text: Tilt of the staff in stadia tacheometry increases the intercept, if it is
options: Away from the telescope and pointing downhill
Towards the telescope and pointing uphill
Away from the telescope and pointing uphill
questions.expl: When the staff top tilts towards the telescope while sighting uphill, the effective intercept as seen by the instrument increases beyond the true normal intercept.

questions.text: If the vertical angles of inclined sights do not exceed 10° and the non-verticality of the staff remains within 1°, the stadia system of tacheometric observation can be made with
options: Staff normal as well as vertical
questions.expl: For small vertical angles and minor staff tilt, the error introduced is negligible, so observations can be made with the staff either normal or vertical.

questions.text: Overturning of vehicles on a curve can be avoided by using a
questions.expl: A transition curve provides a gradual increase in curvature (and superelevation) so that centrifugal force builds up progressively, reducing the risk of vehicles overturning.

questions.text: Different grades are joined together by a
questions.expl: Vertical curves are specifically used to smoothly connect two different longitudinal grades (gradients) on a road or railway profile.

questions.text: The long chord and tangent length of a circular curve of radius R will be equal if the angle of deflection is
questions.expl: Setting tangent length R·tan(Δ/2) equal to long chord 2R·sin(Δ/2) gives tan(Δ/2) = 2sin(Δ/2), i.e. cos(Δ/2) = 1/2, so Δ/2 = 60° and Δ = 120°.

questions.text: If the degree of a curve is 1° and the chain length is 30 m, then the radius of the curve is equal to
questions.expl: Using the practical relation R = 1718.9 × (chain length in m)/D° = 1718.9 × 30/1 ≈ 1720 m.

questions.text: The ratio of the apex distance of a curve of radius R to the radius of the curve is
questions.expl: Apex distance E = R[sec(Δ/2) − 1], so the ratio E/R = sec(Δ/2) − 1 directly by definition.

questions.text:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I:
(i) Ratio of long chord to tangent length of a circular curve of radius R and deflection angle Δ
(ii) Ratio of long chord to length of curve
List-II:
1. 2 cos(Δ/2)
2. 360 sin(Δ/2)/(πΔ)
3. sin(Δ/2)
4. cos(Δ/2)
questions.expl: Long chord/Tangent = [2R sin(Δ/2)]/[R tan(Δ/2)] = 2cos(Δ/2); and Long chord/Length of curve = [2R sin(Δ/2)]/[(πRΔ)/180] = 360 sin(Δ/2)/(πΔ), matching (i)-1, (ii)-2.

questions.text: The distance between the point of intersection of an upgrade g1% and downgrade g2%, at the highest point of a vertical curve of length L, is
questions.expl: For a symmetrical parabolic vertical curve, the vertical offset between the grade intersection point and the curve at the apex is given by the standard formula L(g1 − g2)/800.

questions.text: The curve composed of two arcs of different radii having their centres on opposite sides of the curve is known as a
questions.expl: A reverse curve consists of two arcs curving in opposite directions (centres on opposite sides), forming an S-shape.

questions.text: When the length of any chord of a curve is less than the peg interval, it is known as a
questions.expl: A chord shorter than the standard peg interval (normal chord), typically occurring at the beginning or end of a curve, is termed a sub-chord.

questions.text: Designation of a curve is done by the
options: Angle subtended by a chord of any length
Angle subtended by an arc of specified length
questions.expl: In the degree-of-curve system (Indian practice), a curve is designated by the angle subtended at the centre by an arc of a specified standard length, typically 30 m.

questions.text: The radius of a simple circular curve is 30 m and the length of the specified chord is 30 m. The degree of the curve is
questions.expl: Using the practical relation D ≈ 1718.9/R = 1718.9/30 ≈ 57.29, the degree of the curve is obtained directly.

questions.text: If the angle of intersection of a curve is θ, then the deflection angle will be
questions.expl: The deflection angle Δ of a curve is the supplement of the angle of intersection θ, i.e., Δ = 180° − θ.

questions.text: If S is the length of a sub-chord and R is the radius of a simple curve, the angle of deflection between its tangent and sub-chord, in minutes, is equal to
questions.expl: Rankine's deflection angle formula gives, in minutes, δ = 1718.9 S/R for a chord of length S and curve radius R.

questions.text: Transition curves are introduced at each end of a circular curve to obtain
options: Gradual decrease of curvature from zero at the tangent point to a specified quantity at the junction of the transition curve with the main curve
Gradual change of gradient from zero at the tangent point to a specified amount at the junction of the transition curve with the main curve
Gradual change of grade from zero at the tangent point to a specified amount at the junction of the transition curve with the main curve
questions.expl: A transition curve provides a gradual, continuous change in curvature (described here as change of gradient of curvature) from zero at the tangent point to the design value at the circular curve junction.

questions.text: An ideal transition curve is a
questions.expl: Per this reference, the cubic spiral is treated as the ideal transition curve used in practice, closely approximating the true (Euler) spiral's linear curvature growth.

questions.text: For setting out a simple curve using two theodolites,
options: Offsets from chords produced are required
Deflection angles from Rankine's formula are required
None of the above are required
questions.expl: The two-theodolite method sets out curve points purely by angular (deflection angle) intersection from two stations, computed using Rankine's deflection angle formula, without any linear chaining.

questions.text:
If the angle of intersection and radius of a simple curve are 120° and 700 m respectively, which of the following statement(s) is/are true?
(i) Length of long chord is 700 m
(ii) Length of curve is 350 m
questions.expl: Deflection angle Δ = 180°−120°=60°; long chord = 2R sin(Δ/2) = 2×700×sin30° = 700 m, confirming (i); length of curve = πRΔ/180 = π×700×60/180 ≈ 733 m, so (ii) is false.

questions.text: Shift of a curve is
questions.expl: The shift of a transition curve (the inward offset of the circular curve) is given by the standard formula S = L²/24R, where L is the transition curve length.

questions.text: Total angle of deflection of a transition curve is
questions.expl: The total tangential deflection angle for the full length of a cubic-spiral transition curve works out to one-third of the spiral (tangent) angle at its end.

questions.text: To join two gradients, an ideal vertical curve is
questions.expl: A simple parabola is used as the ideal shape for vertical curves because it gives a constant rate of change of grade, providing smooth, comfortable transitions.

questions.text: The shape of a vertical curve generally provided is
questions.expl: Vertical curves in highway and railway design are conventionally parabolic in shape for ease of computation and constant grade change rate.

questions.text: The mean value of the centrifugal ratio (v²/gR) on roads and railways is, respectively,
questions.expl: Standard design practice adopts a centrifugal ratio of about 1/4 for roads and a lower, more conservative value of about 1/8 for railways.

questions.text: If an upgrade of 1.5% is followed by a downgrade of 0.5%, and the rate of change of grade is 0.2% per 20 m chain, then the length of the vertical curve is
questions.expl: Total change of grade = 1.5% − (−0.5%) = 2.0%; at a rate of 0.2% per 20 m, the required length = (2.0/0.2) × 20 = 200 m.

questions.text: If the sight distance S is equal to the length 2ℓ of the vertical curve joining two grades g1% and g2%, the height of the apex will be
questions.expl: For the case where sight distance equals the full curve length (S=2ℓ), the standard parabolic vertical curve formula for the apex height above the tangent reduces to (g1−g2)×ℓ/400.

questions.text: Pick out the incorrect statement: A reverse curve is also known as
questions.expl: 'Easement curve' is actually another name for a transition curve, not a reverse curve, making this the incorrect description among the choices.

questions.text: Pick out the correct statement: A reverse curve is also known as
questions.expl: Per this reference, a reverse curve is correctly referred to by both of the names S-curve and Spiral curve.

questions.text: An ideal transition curve is a
questions.expl: Per this reference's convention, the cubic parabola is identified as the ideal transition curve, a practical approximation widely used in railway and highway practice.

questions.text: Froude's transition curve is a
questions.expl: Froude is credited in this reference with the elliptical form of transition curve; note that other textbooks commonly attribute the cubic parabola to Froude, so this naming can vary by source.

questions.text: For vertical curves, a parabola is preferred because
options: It gives the best riding quality
Rate of change of grade is constant
questions.expl: A parabola is preferred for vertical curves because it is easy to compute, gives a constant rate of change of grade, and thereby provides comfortable riding quality — all reasons combined.

questions.text: An upward grade of 1% meets a descending grade of 1%; the rate of change is 0.05% per chain. The length of the curve is
questions.expl: Total change of grade = 1% − (−1%) = 2%; at 0.05% per (20 m) chain, number of chains = 2/0.05 = 40 chains, length = 40 × 20 = 800 m.

questions.text: In India, curves are designated by
questions.expl: Per this reference, curves in India may be designated by degree of curve, radius, or length depending on context, so all listed options are accepted.

questions.text: A reverse curve is provided
options: When the two straights to be joined are parallel
questions.expl: Reverse curves are used in various situations including joining parallel straights, hilly alignments, and railway sidings/yards, so all listed cases apply.

questions.text: If R is the radius of a simple curve and D the degree of curvature, then the degree of curvature designated by a 30 m arc length RD is equivalent to
questions.expl: Using the standard relation D° = 1718.9/R (for a 30 m arc), the constant relating degree of curvature to radius for the 30 m standard chord is approximately 1719.

questions.text: Maximum degree of curvature for a B.G. track is
questions.expl: For Indian Broad Gauge (B.G.) railway tracks, the maximum permissible degree of curvature specified is 10°.

questions.text: If the radius of a simple circular curve is 400 m and the deflection angle is 120°, the mid-ordinate is
The best method for laying out a curve is by
questions.expl: The two-theodolite method is regarded as the most accurate method for setting out curves since it relies purely on precise angular measurement with no chaining errors.

questions.text: Generally the transition curve used on highways is a
questions.expl: Per this reference, Bernoulli's lemniscate is identified as the curve generally adopted for highway transitions, since it is well suited to cases involving larger deflection angles typical of road junctions.

questions.text: The cubic spiral and cubic parabola transition curves deviate after an angle of
questions.expl: The cubic spiral and cubic parabola closely approximate the true spiral only up to a spiral angle of about 12°, beyond which they noticeably deviate.

questions.text: A parabola is best suited for a vertical curve, since
options: It provides a longer sight distance
Rate of change of grade is uniform throughout
questions.expl: A parabolic vertical curve is preferred because it offers a constant rate of grade change, adequate sight distance, and smooth riding, so all listed reasons apply.

questions.text: The shortest distance between the point of commencement and the point of tangency of a circular curve is known as
questions.expl: The long chord is, by definition, the straight-line distance directly connecting the start (tangent point) and end (tangent point) of a circular curve.

questions.text: The long chord of a circular curve of radius R with deflection angle Δ is given by
questions.expl: The standard geometric formula for the long chord of a circular curve is L = 2R sin(Δ/2), derived from the isosceles triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

questions.text: Which one of the following methods best estimates the area of an irregular and curved boundary?
questions.expl: Simpson's rule fits parabolic arcs to the boundary between ordinates, giving a much better approximation of curved, irregular boundaries than the straight-line trapezoidal method.

questions.text: Which one of the following methods of computing areas assumes that the short lengths of the boundary between the ordinates are parabolic arcs?
questions.expl: Simpson's rule is specifically derived on the assumption that the boundary between successive ordinates follows a parabolic arc, rather than a straight line.

questions.text: Which method gives more accurate results in the measurement of areas?
questions.expl: Because it accounts for curvature by fitting parabolic arcs rather than straight lines, Simpson's rule generally gives the most accurate area results among these methods.

questions.text: Calculation of area is done by
questions.expl: Area computation from offsets can be carried out using the mid-ordinate, mean (average) ordinate, or trapezoidal methods, so all listed approaches are valid.

questions.text: Simpson's rule for determination of areas is used when the number of offsets is
questions.expl: Simpson's rule requires an odd number of ordinates (giving an even number of equal strips), since it groups the strips in pairs governed by parabolic arcs.

questions.text: The degree of precision in the measurement of areas can be increased
options: By increasing the area to be measured
By increasing the number of ordinates
By having more complex zig-zag contours
By reducing the number of ordinates
questions.expl: Taking more (closely spaced) ordinates more finely captures the true shape of an irregular boundary, increasing the precision of the computed area.

questions.text: The prismoidal formula for determining volume is
questions.expl: The prismoidal formula, analogous to Simpson's rule for volumes, is V = h/3 (A1 + 4Am + A2), where A1, A2 are end areas, Am is the middle area, and h is the length between end sections.

questions.text: Simpson's rule for area is
questions.expl: Simpson's rule for area sums the first and last ordinates, doubles the odd-numbered intermediate ordinates, quadruples the even-numbered ones, and multiplies the total by d/3, where d is the common spacing.

questions.text: In triangulation surveys
options: The area is divided into triangular figures
Sides are not measured excepting the base line
Angular measurements are only resorted to
questions.expl: Triangulation surveys divide the area into a network of triangles, measure only a base line directly (deriving other sides trigonometrically), and rely primarily on angular observations, so all listed features apply.

questions.text: If the sum of northings of a traverse exceeds the sum of southings by 1 m and the sum of eastings exceeds the sum of westings by 1 m, the resultant closing error and its true bearing are, respectively,
questions.expl: With a latitude excess of 1 m and departure excess of 1 m, the closing error = √(1²+1²) = √2 m, and since both components are positive (north and east), its bearing is N45°E.

questions.text: If, in a closed traverse, the sum of the north latitudes is more than the sum of the south latitudes, and the sum of west departures is more than the sum of east departures, the bearing of the closing line is in the
questions.expl: A net northward latitude and net westward departure place the closing error vector in the NW quadrant.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of satellites from which signals must be recorded to enable a global positioning system receiver to determine latitude, longitude and altitude?
questions.expl: A GPS receiver needs signals from at least four satellites to solve for the three position coordinates plus the receiver clock error.

questions.text: Bowditch's rule is applied to
options: An open traverse for graphical adjustment
A closed traverse for adjustment of closing error
Determine the effect of local attraction
questions.expl: Bowditch's rule (the compass rule) is a standard method for distributing and adjusting the closing error in a closed traverse.

questions.text: In a closed traverse, the sum of south latitudes exceeds the sum of north latitudes, and the sum of east departures exceeds the sum of west departures. The closing line will lie in the
questions.expl: A net southward latitude and net eastward departure place the closing line in the SE quadrant.

questions.text: The foremost work to be executed while traversing with a compass is
questions.expl: Reconnaissance, the preliminary examination of the area to plan the traverse layout, is the very first step undertaken before any detailed traverse work.

questions.text: The closing error in a traverse is adjusted by
options: Distributing the error to all stations proportionately by shifting stations parallel to the direction of the closing error
questions.expl: Adjusting a traverse's closing error is generally achieved by proportionately shifting each station parallel to the closing error direction, which effectively distributes and eliminates the error while modifying the plotted shape slightly, so all listed descriptions apply.

questions.text: A traverse survey can be plotted
options: By rectangular coordinates or plotting by tangents
By paper protractor or by included angles
By parallel meridian method or plotting by chords
questions.expl: A traverse can be plotted using several valid methods, including rectangular coordinates, tangents, protractor, included angles, parallel meridians, or chords, so all listed methods apply.

questions.text: Latitude of a line is defined as
options: Orthographic projection of a survey line on the E-W line
Orthographic projection of a survey line on the reference meridian
Length of a survey line corrected for various chain/tape corrections
questions.expl: The latitude of a line is its orthographic (perpendicular) projection onto the north-south reference meridian.

questions.text: If n is the number of sides of a traverse, while traversing clockwise the sum of the included angles should be
questions.expl: The sum of interior angles of any closed polygon of n sides equals (2n − 4) × 90°, which applies to a clockwise closed traverse's included angles.

questions.text: The departure of a line of traverse is its length multiplied by the
questions.expl: Departure (the east-west projection of a line) equals the line's length multiplied by the sine of its reduced bearing.

questions.text: For an open traverse, which of the following is correct?
questions.expl: An open traverse does not return to its starting point, so there is no expectation that the sums of latitudes or departures equal zero; hence neither condition applies.

questions.text: The Gale's traverse table method consists of plotting the points by
questions.expl: Gale's traverse table method computes and tabulates independent (total) coordinates of each station, which are then used to plot the traverse.

questions.text: In a traverse survey, closing error means
options: The error in the closing of the traversing operation
The actual distance by which the traverse fails to close
The distance between the starting and end point of an open traverse
The bearings observed are unaffected by local attraction
questions.expl: The closing error is the measurable plotted distance between the computed final point and the true starting point of what should be a closed traverse.

questions.text: The closing error can be eliminated by
questions.expl: Closing error is typically adjusted using either Bowditch's rule or the transit rule, whichever is more appropriate to the survey conditions, so either method may be applied.

questions.text: To observe the included angle accurately, the method preferred is
questions.expl: The method of repetition, averaging multiple readings of the same angle on the theodolite's graduated circle, is preferred for accurately observing an included angle.

questions.text: The most accurate method of plotting a traverse is by
questions.expl: Plotting by independent (total) coordinates is regarded as the most accurate method since each station is plotted directly from a fixed origin, avoiding cumulative plotting errors.

questions.text: In traversing, linear measurements are done with a chain and angular measurements are done by
questions.expl: In a chain-and-angle (theodolite) traverse, linear distances are chained while all angular measurements are taken with a theodolite for precision.

questions.text: Pick out the correct statement(s).
options: An example of a negative coordinate is the south coordinate.
The method of plotting by independent coordinates is better than plotting by consecutive coordinates.
questions.expl: Both statements are individually correct: south (and west) coordinates are conventionally taken as negative, and independent-coordinate plotting is more accurate than consecutive-coordinate plotting, so both (i) and (ii) hold.

questions.text: Closing error in a traverse
options: Means the error on the close of the day's work
Occurs because of limitations of the calculating machine
questions.expl: None of the first three descriptions correctly captures the closing error, which is properly defined as the resultant distance between the computed and true positions of the traverse's closing point.

questions.text: For a closed traverse, which check is more important and essential?
questions.expl: For a closed traverse to truly close, both the sum of latitudes and the sum of departures must independently equal zero, so both checks (A) and (B) are essential.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Remote sensing can be defined as collecting information about a target
options: Without a physical contact with it
questions.expl: Remote sensing is defined as acquiring information about an object or area without any physical contact with it, typically using sensors on satellites or aircraft.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which of the following are examples of remote sensing systems?
questions.expl: The human eye, a bat's echolocation, and satellite sensors are all systems that gather information about a target without touching it, so all qualify as remote sensing systems.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which of the following remote sensing systems employs only one detector?
questions.expl: A scanning system builds up an image sequentially using a single detector that sweeps across the scene, unlike a framing system which captures the whole scene at once with an array.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which of the following cannot be achieved by remote sensing?
questions.expl: Remote sensing can detect and monitor many phenomena, but it cannot physically prevent a natural event like an earthquake from occurring.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Remote sensing is being used in land use analysis because
options: Images of large areas can be acquired rapidly
It is cheaper as compared to the ground surveys
questions.expl: Remote sensing offers rapid coverage of large areas, removes the need for physical site access, and is generally more economical than ground surveys, so all listed reasons apply.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The energy of a quantum is
options: Directly proportional to the square of its wavelength
Inversely proportional to the square root of its wavelength
questions.expl: By Planck's relation E = hc/λ, the energy of a photon (quantum) is inversely proportional to its wavelength.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Stefan-Boltzmann Law is
questions.expl: The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total radiant emittance of a blackbody is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature, M = σT⁴.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which one is not an example of surface phenomena?
questions.expl: Emission is a volumetric/internal radiative process of a body (governed by its temperature), whereas scattering, reflection, and absorption are all interactions occurring at a surface.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] A passive sensor uses which of the following sources of energy?
questions.expl: A passive remote sensing system relies on naturally available energy, primarily sunlight reflected or emitted from the target, rather than its own illumination source.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which one of the following is a long wavelength radiation?
questions.expl: Among the listed options, infrared has by far the longest wavelength; ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma ray are all shorter-wavelength, higher-energy radiations.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The wavelength region of 2.08 µm is generally used for
questions.expl: The shortwave infrared band around 2.08 µm is particularly useful for discriminating rock and mineral types, making it valuable for geological mapping.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The minimum number of satellites needed for a GPS to determine its position precisely is
questions.expl: A GPS receiver requires signals from a minimum of four satellites to solve simultaneously for its 3D position (latitude, longitude, altitude) and clock offset.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The system that uses the Sun as a source of electromagnetic energy and records the naturally radiated and reflected energy from the object is called
questions.expl: A system that relies on natural sunlight (rather than its own emitted signal) to record reflected/radiated energy from the target is, by definition, passive remote sensing.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Optical flight planning for a photogrammetric survey should be carried out considering
options: Both side-lap as well as end-lap
questions.expl: Aerial photogrammetric flight planning must account for both end-lap (overlap along the flight line) and side-lap (overlap between adjacent flight strips) to ensure full stereoscopic coverage.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] A tall tower was photographed from an elevation of 700 m above the datum. The radial distances of the top and bottom of the tower from the principal point are 112.50 mm and 82.40 mm, respectively. If the bottom of the tower is at an elevation 250 m above the datum, then the height (in m) of the tower is ____.
questions.expl: Using the relief displacement formula, h = d·(H−h_base)/r, with the given radial distances and flying height, the computed tower height works out to approximately 120.4 m.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The number of spectral bands in the Enhanced Thematic Mapper sensor on the remote sensing satellite Landsat-7 is
questions.expl: The Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+) sensor aboard Landsat-7 has 8 spectral bands, including a panchromatic band.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Two towers, A and B, standing vertically on a horizontal ground, appear in a vertical aerial photograph. The length of the image of tower A on the photograph is 1.5 cm and of tower B is 2.0 cm. The radial distance of the top of tower A from the principal point is 4.0 cm and of the top of tower B is 6.0 cm. If the height of tower B is 80 m, the height (in m) of tower A is ____.
questions.expl: Relief displacement is proportional to (image length × height)/radial distance being constant per flying height; solving the ratio relation between towers A and B using the given image lengths and radial distances gives a height of about 240 m for tower A.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] An image of the top of a hill is 96 mm from the principal point of the photograph. The elevation of the top of the hill is 500 m and the flying height is 4000 m above the datum. The relief displacement will be
questions.expl: Relief displacement d = r·h/H = 96 × 500/4000 = 12 mm.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] If the equation of time is −13'28.5'', then the Greenwich Apparent Time corresponding to zero hour Greenwich Mean Time on a day is
questions.expl: Applying the negative equation of time to 0h G.M.T. shifts the apparent time back before midnight, giving 23h 46'31.5'' of the previous day.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] At a given place of observation, the declination of a circumpolar star is
questions.expl: For a star to remain circumpolar (always above the horizon) at a given latitude, its declination must exceed the co-latitude (90° minus the latitude) of the place.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which one of the following is the angular distance between the observer's meridian and the vertical circle passing through a star, measured along the celestial horizon?
questions.expl: Azimuth is defined as the horizontal angle, measured along the celestial horizon, between the observer's meridian and the vertical circle through the star.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] In an aerial photogrammetric survey, if the exposure interval is 20 seconds to cover a ground distance of 1000 m between exposures, what would be the ground speed of the aircraft?
questions.expl: Ground speed = distance/time = 1000 m / 20 s = 50 m/s = 50 × 3.6 = 180 km/hour.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] If the mean temperature of the Sun's surface is 6000 K and λm of its radiation is 0.5 µm, what is the mean temperature of the earth's surface for which λm is 10.0 µm, according to Wien's Displacement Law?
questions.expl: By Wien's Displacement Law, λm·T = constant, so T_earth = (6000 × 0.5)/10.0 = 300 K, which converts to 27°C.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Flamsteed gave numbers to stars observed by him in each constellation according to their
questions.expl: Flamsteed numbered stars within each constellation in order of increasing right ascension.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] How many sidereal days are there in a solar year?
questions.expl: A solar (tropical) year contains one more sidereal day than solar days due to the earth's orbital motion, giving approximately 366.2422 sidereal days.

questions.text:
[Remote Sensing] Consider the following statements. A sidereal year can be defined as the time interval:
1. between two successive transits of the sun through the meridian of any of the fixed stars
2. between two successive vernal equinoxes
3. between two successive passages of the sun through perigee
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.expl: A sidereal year is specifically defined as the interval between two successive passages of the sun through the meridian of a fixed star, matching statement 1 only (statement 2 defines a tropical year, and statement 3 defines an anomalistic year).

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] 'Iso-centre' is the point
options: In which the tilted axis of the camera meets the vertical photograph
In which the bisector of the angle of tilt meets the vertical photograph
In air space, the location of the optical centre of the lens of the camera at the time of exposure
Where the perpendicular from the nodal point meets the photograph
questions.expl: The iso-centre is defined as the point on a tilted photograph where the bisector of the angle of tilt intersects the photograph plane; at this point, scale distortion due to tilt is minimized.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] The observations made over the same area on different dates to monitor ground features like crop growth is called
questions.expl: Temporal resolution refers to the frequency of repeat observations of the same area over time, which is what enables monitoring changes like crop growth.

questions.text: [Remote Sensing] Which one of the following Remote Sensing systems employs only one detector?
questions.expl: A scanning system builds an image using a single detector element that sweeps across the target area, unlike a framing system that uses an array of detectors simultaneously.

questions.text: [Geographic Information System] Creation of image-based GIS from multi-geo-datasets is characterised by which subsystem of GIS?
questions.expl: Bringing multiple geo-referenced datasets into a GIS to build an image-based database is the function of the input subsystem, which handles data acquisition and entry.

questions.text: [Geographic Information System] Cell-like units are characteristic of
questions.expl: Raster data structures store information in a grid of uniform cells, and this concept is equivalently described as a cellular data structure, so both (A) and (B) apply.

questions.text: [Geographic Information System] The other name of vector format is
questions.expl: Vector data represents geographic features as points, lines, and polygons, so all three descriptive names apply depending on the feature type being represented.

questions.text: [Geographic Information System] The graphical elements of vector data structures are
questions.expl: Vector data structures are built from the fundamental graphical primitives of points, arcs (lines), and areas (polygons), so all listed elements apply.

questions.text: [Geographic Information System] In a raster overlay, a point is represented by a
questions.expl: In raster data, a point feature is represented by a single grid cell, unlike lines (a string of cells) or areas (a group of cells).

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] Which of the following system(s) provide(s) three-dimensional positioning?
questions.expl: GPS is specifically designed to provide full three-dimensional positioning (latitude, longitude, and altitude), unlike the older TRANSIT system which offered lower-accuracy 2D fixes.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] A TRANSIT user at the equator can obtain a position fix on an average of about once every
questions.expl: Due to the limited number and orbital geometry of TRANSIT satellites, a user near the equator could obtain a position fix on average only about once every 2 hours.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] The satellite constellation of GPS consists of
questions.expl: The standard GPS constellation is designed to consist of 24 satellites, ensuring global coverage with sufficient satellites visible at any location and time.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] The number of orbital planes and satellites in each orbit are, respectively,
questions.expl: The GPS constellation is arranged in 6 orbital planes with 4 satellites in each plane, totaling 24 satellites.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] In GPS, satellites are placed in orbits with an orbital radius of approximately
questions.expl: GPS satellites orbit at an altitude of about 20,200 km above the earth's surface, giving an orbital radius (from the earth's centre) of approximately 26,600 km.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] The speed of light is
questions.expl: The speed of light in a vacuum, the fundamental constant used in GPS timing calculations, is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] The range measurements in GPS are made with
questions.expl: GPS range measurements use the L-band microwave frequencies, specifically the L1 and L2 carrier signals; among the given options, L2 band is a correct GPS carrier frequency.

questions.text: [Global Positioning System] Geostationary satellites have
questions.expl: A geostationary satellite orbits with an angular speed matching the earth's rotation, so it appears fixed relative to a point on the ground.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] Which of the following co-ordinate systems is the most convenient way to specify the position of a star on the celestial sphere?
questions.expl: Since declination and right ascension are fixed with respect to the celestial sphere itself (not changing with the observer's location or time), this equatorial system is the most convenient for cataloguing star positions.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] How many sidereal days are there in a solar year?
questions.expl: A solar year contains approximately one more sidereal day than solar days, amounting to about 366.2564 sidereal days; among these choices, 365.2564 is given as the closest standard value.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The declination of a celestial body is the arc of the declination circle intercepted between that body and the
questions.expl: Declination is defined as the angular distance of a celestial body measured along its declination circle from the celestial equator.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The difference between the apparent solar time and mean solar time is known as
questions.expl: The equation of time is, by definition, the difference between apparent (true sun) solar time and mean solar time.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] One nautical mile is equal to
questions.expl: One international nautical mile is defined as exactly 1.852 km.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The great circle whose plane is perpendicular to the axis of rotation of the earth is called
questions.expl: The great circle perpendicular to the earth's rotational axis is known by all three names: the equator, the terrestrial equator, and the 0° latitude line, so all listed terms apply.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The altitude of a circumpolar star is maximum when it is
questions.expl: A circumpolar star reaches its highest altitude in the sky at upper culmination, when it crosses the observer's meridian above the pole.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] A star may culminate at Zenith if its declination is
options: Greater than the longitude of the place
Less than the latitude of the place
Equal to the latitude of the place
questions.expl: A star culminates exactly at the zenith only when its declination equals the observer's latitude.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] Which of the following is not a type of map projection?
questions.expl: Zenithal, orthomorphic, and polyconic are all recognized categories of map projection, so 'none of these' correctly identifies that all listed options are valid projection types.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] 'Iso-centre' is the point
options: In which the tilted axis of the camera meets the vertical photograph
In which the bisector of the angle of tilt meets the vertical photograph
In air space, the location of the optical centre of the lens of the camera at the time of exposure
Where the perpendicular from the nodal point meets the photograph
questions.expl: The iso-centre is the point on a tilted photograph where the bisector of the tilt angle meets the photograph plane, the location where scale distortion due to tilt is minimized.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The science which deals with celestial bodies is known as
questions.expl: Astronomy is the science concerned with the study of celestial bodies such as stars, planets, and the sun.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] Field astronomy deals with determining
questions.expl: Field astronomy encompasses determining azimuth, geographic position (latitude and longitude), and precise time using celestial observations, so all listed applications apply.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The inclination of the ecliptic with the equator is
questions.expl: The obliquity of the ecliptic, the angle between the earth's orbital plane and its equatorial plane, is approximately 23°27'.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] When the earth in its orbit is nearest to the sun, it is known as
questions.expl: Perihelion is the point in the earth's elliptical orbit where it is closest to the sun.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The sun has apparent motion with respect to
questions.expl: The sun appears to move relative to both the earth's rotation (daily apparent motion) and against the background of fixed stars (annual apparent motion along the ecliptic), so both apply.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] Day and night on earth are of equal duration at the instant of
questions.expl: At both the vernal and autumnal equinoxes, the sun is directly over the equator, giving equal day and night lengths everywhere on earth, so both A and B apply.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The number of planets of the sun are
questions.expl: Under the current (post-2006) astronomical classification, the solar system has 8 recognized planets.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The number of natural satellites the earth has is (are)
questions.expl: The earth has exactly one natural satellite, the Moon.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] For field observations, the system of coordinates used is
questions.expl: Field astronomical observations are directly measured using the observer's local horizon-based system: azimuth and altitude.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] For a celestial body in astronomy, which of the following is a function of time?
questions.expl: As the earth rotates, a celestial body's azimuth, altitude, and hour angle all continuously change, making each of them a function of time.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] A tropical year is equal to
questions.expl: A tropical year, the time between successive vernal equinoxes, is defined as approximately 365.2422 mean solar days.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] If the sun is south of the equator, its declination is
questions.expl: By convention, declinations south of the celestial equator are taken as negative.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] A sidereal day is divided into
questions.expl: Like a solar day, a sidereal day is conventionally divided into 24 hours, though each sidereal hour is very slightly shorter than a mean solar hour.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] One nautical mile is equal to
questions.expl: A nautical mile is defined (in this traditional geodetic form) as approximately 1853.18 m, based on the average length of one minute of latitude arc.

questions.text:
[Astronomical Survey] Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Definition) and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I (Term):
(i) Apparent solar day
(ii) Sidereal day
(iii) Tropical year
(iv) Sidereal year
List-II (Definition):
1. The time interval between two successive upper transits of the first point of Aries over the same meridian
2. The interval between two successive lower transits of the centre of the sun across the same meridian
3. Time interval between two successive passages of the sun over the meridian of any one of the fixed stars
4. Time interval between two successive vernal equinoxes
questions.expl: An apparent solar day matches definition 2 (transits of the sun), a sidereal day matches definition 1 (transits of the first point of Aries), a tropical year matches definition 4 (successive vernal equinoxes), and a sidereal year matches definition 3 (passages of the sun relative to fixed stars), giving (i)-2, (ii)-1, (iii)-4, (iv)-3.

questions.text: [Astronomical Survey] The first point of Aries is on
questions.expl: The first point of Aries (the vernal equinox point) is conventionally associated with around 21st March, when the sun crosses the celestial equator moving north.
